chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the Committee on Housing and Buildings hearing, instructs witnesses to fill out witness slips, and asks all to silence electronic devices. Chair Sanchez is confirmed ready to begin.
chapters.title: Staff opens hearing and announces procedures

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to testify, you must fill out a witness slip with one of the sergeant-at-arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all electronic devices and no one may approach the dais at any time.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair Sanchez, we are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Pierina Ana Sanchez welcomes colleagues and the public, frames the hearing around Mayor Mamdani's Block by Block housing plan, and describes the city's profound housing crisis, noting historic low vacancy rates and disproportionate impacts on lowest-income New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez opens oversight hearing on Mayor Mamdani's Block by Block housing plan

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Sergeants, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Pierina Sanchez, Chair of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: On behalf of the City Council, I'd like to welcome the members of the public and the administration that join us today, in person and remotely, for today's oversight hearing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I first want to acknowledge my colleagues who are present, Majority Leader Abreu, Councilmember Hudson, Councilmember Aviles, Councilmember Maloney, Councilmember Nurse, Councilmember Wilson, Banks, Epstein, Thomas Henry, and Aldebol.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Today's hearing is focused on Mayor Zoran Mamdani's Block by Block, the housing plan for a new era.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: A comprehensive vision for empowering tenants, strengthening enforcement, preserving affordability, improving housing quality, expanding homeownership, and more.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We begin from a reality we all know.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: New York City is in a profound housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Our vacancy rate has fallen to historic lows, but this crisis is not experienced equally.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: For the lowest income New Yorkers, housing insecurity can mean a child traveling hours from a shelter

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Queens to remain in their school in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It can mean families living with mold, vermin, insufficient heat, and the constant fear that one missed paycheck could cost them their home.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In my district, where roughly 70% of households are housing cost burdened, this is the reality.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And these inequities did not happen by accident.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Generations of public policies have determined who could own a home, whose neighborhood received investment, and whose wealth could grow.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Today, those same communities face a federal government threatening housing assistance and the basic safety net that keeps families afloat.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's why this plan matters so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And there is so much good in here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: There is a vision of government more willing to stand up to bad actors, more willing to empower tenants, more creative about rescuing distressed buildings, more ambitious about building housing and expanding homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And people are hopeful.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: People who have spent generations watching government work better

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: for people and areas with money and power are wondering whether we could actually ever shift that balance, whether tenants might have more power someday,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: whether working people could finally have a government willing to fight as hard for their stability as others fight for profit, present company included.

chapters.summary: Sanchez calls on the administration to explain implementation details beyond the plan's pages, outlining four questioning areas: agency staffing capacity, preservation strategy distinguishing high-road from low-road landlords, homelessness and voucher programs, and accountability benchmarks. She also notes concern about climate resilience gaps in the plan.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez outlines four areas of questioning: capacity, preservation, homelessness, accountability

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But New Yorkers have heard ambitious promises before.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We have celebrated production targets before, and too often when we look back at what was actually produced, preserved, or made affordable for our lowest-income neighbors, government actually fell painfully short of the moment.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So today, members of the administration, I ask you to...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Give us reason to believe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Explain to us what you could not fit on the 120 pages of block by block or the 70 pages of the rental ripoff report or the 40 pages of the speed report and more.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How will you implement these promises?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: My questions will begin in four places.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: First, capacity.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: A bold housing plan cannot be implemented by understaffed agencies.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If we promise stronger code enforcement, roof-to-cellar inspections, emergency repairs, aggressive litigation and preservation,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: then HPD and Department of Buildings need the inspectors, attorneys, preservation staff, and institutional capacity to deliver.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Second, with respect to preservation, some of our most affordable housing is also our oldest and our most distressed.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We need a government capable of intervening before buildings collapse into crisis.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That means capital and support for responsible owners trying to keep buildings affordable and escalating enforcement against owners who chronically endanger tenants.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So what is your distinction between high road and low road?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Landlords mean in practice.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This council represents tenants, but it also represents responsible owners, all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The effect of the rental arrears crisis for landlords is real.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Housing court delays are real.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Cash flow problems can destabilize otherwise responsible affordable buildings, including affordable co-ops, rent-stabilized housing, and regulated housing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We need a preservation strategy sophisticated enough to recognize those realities.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Third, on homelessness, we spend billions of dollars every year operating a shelter system while families desperately search for permanent homes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In discussing an all-of-the-above approach, the plan does not speak comprehensively to the many housing voucher programs in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: FEPS, HAVP, Section 8, the newly created CHAP.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm going to do that every time I say it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm really glad we didn't go with crap.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: City Rental Assistance Program.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And our other housing resources that could move us towards something bigger, preventing homelessness before it happens.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And finally, accountability.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Plans are only as meaningful as what happens next, so we want the implementation schedules, the measurable benchmarks, and clarity about who to hold responsible if any of the plans fall behind.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I personally, of course, I'm excited to see a focus on the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I also have to mention that I'm concerned about the lack of mention of climate resilience throughout these plans and hope that these preservation and enforcement commitments can work together to address any gaps that we talk about today.

chapters.summary: Sanchez lists the bills under consideration: Intro 178 (Office of Conversion Assistance, Epstein), Intro 649 (owner identification signs, Restler), Intro 717 (permit sign-off notices, Salaam), Intro 860 (street number enforcement, Brewer), Intro 905 (COPA, Nurse), Intro 1015 (J51 reauthorization, Sanchez), and a preconsidered bill on electronic dwelling registration (Banks).
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez introduces seven bills on the hearing agenda

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In addition to our oversight topic, the committee will also hear intro number 178, sponsored by Councilmember Harvey Epstein in relation to establishing an Office of Conversion Assistance.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Intro number 649, sponsored by Councilmember Lincoln Ressler, in relation to requiring the posting of a sign identifying the owners of multiple dwellings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Number 717 by Councilmember Yusef-Salaam, in relation to requiring the Department of Buildings to inform property owners of permit sign-off requirements.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Intro number 8.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 860 sponsored by Councilmember Brewer in relation to the inspection and enforcement of street numbers on buildings and pre-considered T26-1780

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: sponsored by Councilmember Chris Banks in relation to authorizing electronic registration of dwellings with the Department of Housing Preservation and Development.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Perhaps one of the most exciting bills today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They're all great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They're all great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to give the sponsors of these bills an opportunity to speak on their legislation, starting with Councilmember Nurse, followed by Epstein and Banks.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Did I mention 905?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you go ahead, 905.

chapters.summary: Council Member Sandy Nurse presents the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, citing examples of distressed buildings in the Bronx and Manhattan where landlords use deterioration as a strategy to push tenants out. She explains COPA would give mission-driven nonprofits the first right to purchase at-risk buildings before speculators.
chapters.title: CM Nurse presents COPA (Intro 905) as tool to combat speculative displacement

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez, for hosting this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: New Yorkers are living through a cost of living crisis decades in the making, and housing sits at the center of it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Working class and middle income families are competing for fewer and fewer units every year, and landlords know it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: This drives rents higher and allows bad conditions to fester.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yes, we need to build more housing, but I fundamentally disagree with a purely market-driven approach.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The fact is the private market cannot create enough affordable housing to solve this crisis, especially if we're losing the affordable housing stock we do have faster than we can build.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And that's where the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act comes in.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: This bill is about interrupting a cycle of despair and neglect by design.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Because many landlords across this city use deterioration as a strategy to get their tenants out.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We can look at buildings like 2076 Creston Avenue in the Bronx, a 41-unit building that has racked up over 2,000 violations despite being passed from owner to owner while tenants remain living in untenable conditions.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We can look to Manhattan at 331 East 14th Street, a 20-unit building with 358 BNC violations bought by a private equity firm that has let the building rot, betting that tenants will simply give up and leave.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Once passed, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act will give Mission

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: driven, vetted nonprofits the first right to make an offer on these distressed buildings before speculators can.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It brings these buildings into community ownership and public oversight.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It keeps rents affordable and most importantly it keeps people in their homes, near their schools, their jobs, their support systems and their lives.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: 62% of New Yorkers, about 5 million people, are not able to meet the basic cost of living in our city.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Over 70% of New York City children are growing up in households that cannot make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And meanwhile, the top 1% has never had it so good.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Every affordable unit we lose is a family that is either going to shelter or finally leaving the city.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And we need to put every option on the table to give families a chance.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The Community Opportunity to Purchase Act does that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The bill version we are discussing today is the result of dozens of conversations with stakeholders who are both for and against this bill, many of whom are here today.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I really look forward to the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I want to thank you, Chair Sanchez, Speaker Menon, HPD, the COPA Coalition, and everyone who gave us feedback and helped us shape this bill.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And this is the third time we are hearing this bill together as colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's the charm.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's the charm.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I truly believe in this piece of legislation, and I'm excited about the discussion today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Next, I want to call on Councilmember Epstein to talk about this bill.

chapters.summary: Council Member Harvey Epstein describes his bill to establish an Office of Conversion Assistance to facilitate office-to-residential conversions, noting that one-third of new housing permits this year came from conversions. He references the 234 East 42nd Street partial collapse as underscoring the need for technical support.
chapters.title: CM Epstein presents Intro 178 to create Office of Conversion Assistance

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez, for your leadership and my colleagues on the Housing Committee for an important hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: As we all know, New Yorkers are facing a historic housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: According to the most recent 2024 Housing and Vacancy Survey, the vacancy rate 1.4%, less than 1% for rent-stabilized units in the city, the lowest level ever recorded.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Office to residential conversion presents a significant opportunity to expand our housing supply.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: According to Department of Buildings records, about one-third of new housing permits have come from these conversions this year.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: However, many developers still struggle to navigate the process of conversion because it involves construction and reconstruction of entire floors, potentially demolishing the entire building interior, courtyard, light, additional stories potentially on top of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: At the same time, the unusual partial collapse at 234 East 42nd Street shows a critical need for more technical support to prevent future dangerous incidents.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: My bill, Introduction 178, is meant to unlock the true power of these conversions.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: by creating an office of conversion assistance to facilitate the conversion process by advising those interested in converting property, liaison with relevant agency, all the government level, and reporting data on these conversions.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This resource can ensure this type of conversion is safe as possible.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: In addition to providing assistance with the process, the reporting mandates by this bill is important to identify barriers to conversion process and finding ways to address them.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We must ensure that we're meeting the housing crisis with real solutions to increase the affordable housing supply and the housing supply in general.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration, testifying from advocates as well, and all the New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I want to thank the chair and Speaker Menendez for having this opportunity today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Now we'll hear from Councilmember Banks.

chapters.summary: Council Member Chris Banks presents his preconsidered bill to allow electronic registration of dwellings with HPD, citing property owners' experiences of paper registrations being lost while the $13 fee was always cashed. He describes the bill as modernizing a routine government process for the 21st century.
chapters.title: CM Banks presents electronic property registration bill

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This is a very straightforward bill, common sense piece of legislation that will modernize and update the process that makes it easier for property owners to comply with city requirements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: After hearing property owners and advocates and organizations such as the small property owners of New York, it has become clear that the current paper-based registration system creates unnecessary challenges.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, property owners shared experiences of submitting registration paperwork on time, sometimes even by certified mail, only to be told later that the documents could not be located.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: and would need to be resubmitted.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: At the same time, many noted that while the paperwork seemed to go missing, the $13 registration fee did not.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The legislation provides for a practical solution by allowing property owners to register their properties electronically through an online system maintained by HPD,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: and it would permit the use of electronic signatures, allow filing fees to be paid online and create a more efficient and reliable registration process

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: while preserving a transition period for paper submissions.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By moving this process online, we can reduce the administrative burdens,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: improve record keeping, minimize the risk of lost paperwork, and provide confirmation that submissions have been received and increase accountability for both the property owner and the agency.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Ultimately, this bill is about bringing a routine government process into the 21st century and ensuring that property owners can interact with city government in a way that is efficient and transparent and reliable.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Again, I want to thank the chair and my staff and the ledge team for working with my office to bring this bill and the advocates from Sponey and property owners who worked with my office on this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We're looking forward to hearing the testimonies today.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And again, thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Banks, and shout out to you for being so collaborative and just willing to talk about all the ways to strengthen this bill.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that we were joined briefly by Councilmember Joseph, who will be back.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And next, we're going to hear from our public advocate, who has just joined us.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I'm surprising, so I'm going to keep talking until he's ready.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Public advocate, Jumaane Williams.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Williams praises the plan as one of the better housing plans across administrations, highlighting the $22 billion commitment, 200,000 new and 200,000 preserved units, Bronx investments, and the SPEED Task Force. He urges passage of COPA and Intro 717, and raises concerns about NYCHA management alongside funding.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams testifies on Block by Block plan and bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's just great to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I just, I'm sitting here across the desk from people that I used to organize with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So that's pretty amazing, except it just shows that we're a lot older than we used to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But it's just an honor to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Good morning again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My name is Jermaine Williams, Public Advocate of the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Sanchez and the members of the Committee on Housing and Buildings for holding this hearing and for the administration for being here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Block by Block, the administration's premier plan for tackling the housing crisis in New York City, is a comprehensive, multi-pronged approach that emphasizes tenant empowerment, strengthening enforcement mechanisms, reducing and preventing homelessness, and stabilizing homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: With more than $22 billion committed for the next five years, this plan seeks to deliver 200,000 new affordable units and further preserving 200,000 existing homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: A dedicated $1 billion will be allocated towards supportive housing in the next two years, shoring up vital resources at a time when federal cuts threaten to close doors and destabilize housing for some of our most vulnerable New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Block by Block also spotlights new investments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: in the Bronx where housing quality and stability issues have been exacerbated by a series of devastating fires and partial collapses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The Bronx has historically had the highest eviction filings per month, a trend that's held true from before the pandemic through today, paired with persistent housing maintenance problems which increased citywide in the first four months of FY26, according to the preliminary mayor's management report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These trends convey the inequity of housing needs that exist in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I look forward to seeing the work that comes out of the new Bronx Planning Coalition expected to form this fall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The streamlining procedures to expedite equitable development or speed task force established under Executive Order 5 will not only ensure we are building off the success of City of Yes, but also going back and identifying where we can do better and be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Decades of underbuilding have left New York City with a dire housing shortage, and while construction has picked up and new opportunities such as office to residential conversions and accessory dwelling units are providing some relief, inflation and ongoing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: international conflicts continue to impact the supply chain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Pursuing new innovative approaches to lowering construction costs will help bridge this gap in housing needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Finally, there's a lot of great bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to briefly uplift Intro 904 and Intro 717, for which I am a proud co-sponsor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Intro 905, the Community Purchase Act, COPA, would allow qualified entities the first opportunity to submit a statement of interest and purchase certain properties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Until 7-17, we require the Department of Buildings to inform property owners of permit sign-on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: of requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Together, these bills serve the purpose of strengthening the administration's goal of preserving affordable housing, advancing racial equity, and further supporting homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I look forward to working with the administration implementing this plan and ensuring that New Yorkers have access to deeply affordable, quality housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm also hoping, and I like the part that's in there about NYCHA, but I would like to know how that money is going to be spent to fix the problems and what we're going to do to make management much better because it's a two-pronged approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We need the money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We also need better management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, public advocate and former chair of the Committee on Housing and Building.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks her committee and personal staff by name, then committee counsel administers the oath to the administration witnesses preparing to testify.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez acknowledges staff and administers oath to administration witnesses

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to take this opportunity to thank my team, of course, our deputy chiefs, Ben Ratner for policy, Kim Castellanos, Maria Jose Mares,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: as well as the rest of our team, Gerard Fernandez, Dylan Campos, Soraya Bonilla, Oriana Roa Acevedo, and Marcus Khan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the Housing and Buildings Committee staff who prepared all the materials for today, Senior Legislative Counsel Austin Malone.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Legislative Council Billy X, Senior Policy Analyst Jose Conde, Policy Analyst Dirk Spencer, Data Scientist Mohamed Shadid and Noah Schlossberg, and Finance Analyst Carla Naranjo and Spencer Kuhn.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I will now turn it to our Committee Council to administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and to answer all council member questions honestly?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Commissioner Dina Levy introduces the administration's testimony, outlining four priorities: tenant protections and code enforcement, building 200,000 new affordable units over 10 years, preserving 200,000 existing units, and building equitable neighborhoods including a targeted Bronx plan.
chapters.title: HPD Commissioner Levy outlines four core priorities of Block by Block plan

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Sanchez, members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Thank you for having me back.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I am pleased to be here today to testify regarding Mayor Mamdani's bold housing plan, Block by Block.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The plan lays out a comprehensive strategy to address New York's housing crisis at the scale and with the urgency it deserves.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Today I would like to focus on four core priorities outlined in the plan.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: First is our administration's commitment to ensuring that we are providing protections for tenants and significantly improving our enforcement, code enforcement efforts.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Second is our commitment to building a record amount of affordable housing with the goal of building 200,000 new units over the next 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are also committed to preserving and stabilizing an additional 200,000 units over the same period, as well as using creative interventions that will drive down operating expenses and bring stability to responsible landlords and their tenants.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Third is a focus on building more equitable neighborhoods, including doubling our production of new homeownership units over the next two years,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: meeting our fair housing goals, and making sure we are investing not only in affordable housing, but also in healthy neighborhoods, starting with our targeted Bronx plan.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Finally, in every aspect of this work, there is our commitment to delivering public excellence.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: This includes significantly improving the housing lottery system, working with our partner agencies to eliminate redundancies in permitting and approvals,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: and improving communication and work streams with external partners through initiatives like the tools program and clarifying HPD's priorities with respect to our production pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We have already made progress towards all of these goals, but there is much more to come.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would like to start with our commitment to improving protections for tenants and strengthening enforcement.

chapters.summary: Levy describes the Fix the City initiative targeting 10 highly distressed portfolios, a new OCA directive expediting hearings for vacate order and 7A cases to five days, new heat complaint inspection protocols for the upcoming heat season, and a new code inspection scheduling system for failed access attempts.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levy details Fix the City enforcement initiative and OCA agreement

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Since I last testified, we have launched Fix the City, a new initiative focused on combating historically and chronically negligent landlords.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Fix the City is leveraging a range of tools to increase enforcement efforts against 10 highly distressed portfolios, and we are working in partnership with the Department of Buildings and the Mayor's Office to protect tenants, as well as the Law Department, to advance this effort.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: At the end of August, we announced a major step forward in partnership with the Office of Court Administration.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Under a new directive with regard to litigation brought against buildings subject to vacate orders, cases seeking 7A administrators, and comprehensive cases where essential services have been cut off to more than one-third of the building,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: OCA has directed judges to schedule hearings within five days and to adjudicate these cases on an expedited timeline, granting adjournments only under extreme circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: In July's rental ripoff,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: report, we outlined a series of policy recommendations to improve HPD's 311 protocols.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: For the first time this heat season, HPD will investigate all unit-specific heat complaints rather than a sample of units from a single building.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And starting this fall, HPD will launch a new code inspection protocol for circumstances when attempts to gain access are unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Under the new system, tenants may receive a message allowing them to call HPD and schedule a second inspection at a specific time and date.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are also looking forward to working with the Council to explore improvements to the Housing Maintenance Code, including how we address pest infestation, mold remediation, and revisiting what types of violations justify legally withholding rent.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The agencies have been meeting internally, and we will launch regular convenings with members of the council and external stakeholders later this month.

chapters.summary: Levy details the $100 million city-backed insurance program (22 RFEI responses received, goal of 20,000 homes by end of 2027), the tools program offering low-cost interventions for HPD-regulated building owners, and collaboration with tenant associations on acquisition and rehabilitation of at-risk rent-stabilized portfolios.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levy on landlord support: insurance program, tools program, tenant association partnerships

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: While enforcement is a top priority, HPD is fully committed to supporting well-intentioned landlords who are struggling to maintain their buildings in light of escalating operating costs such as insurance and ongoing challenges with rent collection.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As previously discussed, we have issued a request for expressions of interest to identify a partner for a $100 million city-backed insurance program.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As of the August deadline, we have received 22 responses, and we are on track to select one or more partners by the end of the calendar year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Our goal will be to insure 20,000 homes by the end of next year,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: and 100,000 homes by the end of next year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We have also launched the tools program which allows HPD regulated building owners to request low or no cost interventions to help stabilize and improve the physical and financial health of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That includes expedited access to building reserves, comprehensive code violation clearance, and pro bono technical assistance offered by three partnering organizations, Enterprise, LISC, and the New York City Housing Partnership.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Lastly, we have been collaborating with organized tenant associations to advance acquisition and rehabilitation of at-risk rent-stabilized portfolios, particularly those facing bankruptcy and foreclosure.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Using existing HPD preservation tools, we are working with tenant-supported preservation buyers whose interventions will restore stability and bring long-term affordability back to hundreds of units of rent-stabilized housing.

chapters.summary: Levy outlines production goals of 28,000 affordable homes over two fiscal years including 8,000 extremely/very low-income units, plans to double Open Door homeownership production, launch the Our Home term sheet for cooperative conversions, and increase Home First down payment assistance to serve 600 homebuyers.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levy on housing production targets and homeownership expansion

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Since our June closings, we have been ramping up our new housing production with the goal of building 28,000 affordable homes over the next two fiscal years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: This includes 8,000 units that will serve extremely and very low-income households, 2,000 units dedicated to senior housing, and a 40% increase in the number of households moving out of shelter.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: With respect to homeownership, we are advancing plans to double production of our open door program, launch of the new term sheet for our home, which will support conversion of small and mid-sized rental buildings to limited equity cooperatives, and increase

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: funding for Home First, our down payment assistance program, with the goal of serving 600 homebuyers over the next two years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And we are working with our development partners to clearly communicate HPD priorities with emphasis on cost efficiency, readiness to proceed, advancing our fair housing goals,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: and increasing the number of affordable projects built on publicly owned land.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: By offering our partners clearer communication and greater certainty, we are reducing backlogs in our pipeline and seeing meaningful savings in total development costs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Alongside our partner agencies, we have begun to implement the actions outlined in our speed report

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: port rolled out in May, which include process changes for Housing Connect, with several changes going into effect this fall.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We have increased staff lines for our development team to bring on program liaisons who will ensure that projects are moving through the pipeline quickly and who will assist in cutting through red tape.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are also taking steps to ensure that our neighborhoods are equipped to deal with the impacts of climate change, both in terms of our decarbonization goals and with respect to making neighborhoods more resilient.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As we work to address the devastating loss of housing that occurred in the Hollis community last week,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: HPD and our partners across the city are focused on a multi-pronged approach, utilizing specific building-level interventions such as the READY program and the Resilient Retrofit program, planning for neighborhood-wide green and blue infrastructure investments,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: like those planned for the Jewel Street neighborhood, and working with individual property owners and tenants on options for voluntary buyouts where necessary.

chapters.summary: Levy addresses climate resilience efforts including the Hollis community response, READY and Resilient Retrofit programs. She then states HPD's support for COPA, Intro 1015 (J51 reauthorization), and the other bills on the agenda, noting alignment with preservation goals.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levy on climate resilience, Housing Connect, and bill positions

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I want to take the last few minutes to address the several bills currently under consideration by the Council.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Councilmember Nurse's Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, COPA, will allow capable not-for-profit purchasers to preserve affordable units,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: address hazardous conditions, and avoid speculative transactions that lead to harassment and displacement.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We support this legislation and believe it is aligned with our larger housing preservation goals.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Next, I want to thank Councilmember Sanchez for sponsoring Intro 1015, which will reauthorize the J51 tax incentive.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: J51 is a critical tool to ensuring aging building systems can be upgraded, vacant units can be

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: quickly brought back online, and that both rental buildings and co-ops can make the energy efficiency improvements needed to comply with the mandates under Local Law 97.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We also support the goals of Councilmember Banks'proposed legislation authorizing electronic registration of properties,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Councilmember Ressler's bill on visibly identifying property owners, Councilmember Brewer's legislation on physical street numbers, and Councilmember Epstein's bill to advance commercial conversions.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We look forward to engaging with the Council to ensure that the goals outlined in these legislative proposals are achieved as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As always, I

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I want to thank the Council for your deep commitment and partnership in working to solve the city's housing challenges and for your willingness to work closely with this administration

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: on finding bold and innovative solutions to ensuring that New York City is a decent, safe, and affordable place to live.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify, and I look forward to answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Commissioner Amin Tagani describes DOB's strategic realignment into the housing and planning portfolio, explaining how this positions DOB to leverage data and expertise to remove barriers to affordable housing and advance equity.
chapters.title: DOB Commissioner Tagani on agency realignment with housing portfolio

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Sanchez and members of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: My name is Amin Tagani, and I serve as the Commissioner of the New York City Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I'm joined by DOB subject matter experts from our Enforcement, Development, and Sustainability Bureaus.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to testify regarding Intro 717, which would require DOB to notify property owners when open permits...

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: With open permits that must receive DOB sign-off, and to join my colleagues in government to speak to the mayor's comprehensive block-by-block housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: For DOB, the block-by-block housing plan presented a unique opportunity to collaborate from the ground up, bringing our processes, expertise, and experience to bear in translating the mayor's vision for addressing the housing crisis in a substantive and

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: equitable way and strategy.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: It was an opportunity not only to help shape the plan, but to work alongside other New Yorkers to turn the vision into results.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The groundwork began with a strategically important decision to realign DOB within the administration and move it into the housing and planning portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: As the agency responsible for

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Enforcing the zoning resolution, maintaining the building code, and stewarding the policies that establish the regulatory oversight of more than 1.1 million buildings, DOB has deep and consequential ties to the work of housing and planning.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Bringing the agency into closer alignment with this portfolio created a cleaner, more direct connection between our regulatory responsibilities and the administration's housing priorities.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: It positioned DOB to better leverage our process, our data, our expertise, and day-to-day interactions with the built environment to help remove the barriers that too often stand between New Yorkers and the stability that comes with having an affordable place to call home.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: This alignment was more than an organizational change.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: It was a strategic opportunity to ensure that DOB was not simply regulating the city's buildings, but actively contributing to the broader effort to expand housing opportunity, advance equity, and deliver meaningful results for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Tagani details DOB's Affordable Housing Hub program expansion, the ADU4U initiative launched in partnership with HPD, and the new Affordable and Efficient Code Reform Task Force bringing together government and industry experts to identify building code changes.
chapters.title: Commissioner Tagani on SPEED Task Force, ADU4U, and code reform

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: To that end, DOB continues to advance initiatives and facilitate development across New York City while maintaining the highest safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB was proud to partner with agencies across the city through the SPEED Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: As part of this effort, the department is expanding its Affordable Housing Hub program, assigning the

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB personnel to help HPD projects move more efficiently through the permitting process.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB is also working closely with HPD and the council on shared housing legislation that would increase the number of residential units available to New Yorkers and make better use of existing space.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Similarly, last March, DOB, in partnership with HPD and the mayor's office, introduced ADU4U, an initiative to make it easier for homeowners to add ancillary dwelling units to their properties.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB is working closely with partner agencies to move these initiatives forward.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: In my time in city government, I have never seen this level of coordination, not only with partner agencies and our colleagues in elected office, but with our industry partners as well.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: This coordinated approach includes the establishment of DOB's Affordable and Efficient Code Reform Task Force,

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: which will bring together experts from across government and the construction industry to identify changes to the building code and other relevant regulatory schemes.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The department is excited to collaborate with the agency and industry partners and look forward to working with the council and all responsible parties as we kick off the task force later this month.

chapters.summary: Tagani describes improvements to the DOB NOW online system for job filings and inspections, exploration of drone technology for building inspections, and the launch of the Buildings Tech Lab, a public-private partnership connecting tech companies with DOB experts to develop innovative solutions.
chapters.title: Commissioner Tagani on DOB NOW system, drone technology, and Buildings Tech Lab

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: While expanding the city's housing supply remains an urgent priority, DOB's responsibilities also encompass the commercial development that creates jobs and provides essential services for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We recognize that the department must have the technological capacity to meet these demands.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The department continues to improve our DOB.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: now system, making it easier to process job filings, schedule inspections, and access important building and property information online.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The OB is also working with city agencies, including the Office of Technology and Innovation, to explore how drone technology can support our work around building inspections.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Meanwhile, we're excited to have launched the Buildings Tech Lab, a public-private initiative with a partnership fund for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The Buildings Tech Lab connects technology companies with DOB subject matter experts, giving companies an opportunity to develop and test technologies that can improve the way our department operates.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Public-private partnerships like this will help DOB continue to innovate, respond to an increasingly complex development environment, and advance the city's climate goals.

chapters.summary: Tagani addresses Intro 717, explaining the proposed notification timeline (7 days after permit issuance, every 90 days, then every 2 weeks near expiration). DOB supports the intent but warns that frequent notifications may cause owners to ignore them as spam, and expresses willingness to work with the Council.
chapters.title: Commissioner Tagani on Intro 717 permit sign-off notification bill

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Engaging with our applicants is also a key piece to making the rest of our process improvements more efficient, and something we understand to be the intention of Councilmember Salam's proposed In Show 717.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Under Intro 717, notices would be sent within seven days after a permit is issued and every 90 days thereafter until sign-off is obtained.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: When an open permit is set to expire within 90 days or has expired, DOB would be required to send notices to building owners every two weeks until sign-off is obtained.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: These notices would include the permit number, expiration date, explain the need for sign-off, outline inspection requirements, the consequences of failing to comply, and any additional information DOB deems relevant.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB supports the intent of this bill and recognizes the importance of educating owners regarding the obligation to obtain permit sign-off.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Notices can be a useful tool to reach owners.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: However, the frequency of the proposed notifications, particularly during the 90-day period, may negatively impact their effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Inundating with notices may result in owners ignoring such notices or their email box perceiving them as spam.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We believe education and outreach is the right direction, and we look forward to working with the council on this legislation.

chapters.summary: Tagani reports construction injuries fell 42% from FY24 to FY25, details the Mayor's Committee on Construction Safety, and describes DOB's Office of the Tenant Advocate handling 1,579 inquiries and 487 inspections in 2025. He also describes participation in Fix the City alongside HPD and the law department.
chapters.title: Commissioner Tagani on construction safety statistics and tenant protection

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: As we work to make development faster, more sustainable and efficient, safety remains DOB's top priority.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The department is proud to help lead the Mayor's Committee on Construction Safety alongside the Deputy Mayor for Housing and Planning and the Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The committee will examine the causes of construction-related injuries and fatalities and recommend changes to local laws, agency resources, enforcement practices, and contractor standards to help prevent future accidents.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB's shift to a proactive enforcement model is also helping keep New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Between fiscal year 2024 to fiscal year 2025, construction-related injuries fell by 42%, from 625 to 363.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: This process would not have been possible without the tireless work of more than 100 employees in our construction safety division.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: However, more work remains.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Every injury that happens, we should seek to try to prevent.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: From January through the end of August 2026, there were 232 construction-related injuries and four fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: No injury or fatality at a jab site is acceptable, and DOB remains focused on prevention.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Indeed, DOB-approved course providers have issued approximately 465,000 active site safety training cards, which includes supervisory site training

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: of different types, which equals around 18 million hours of training.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB will continue to enforce requirements and work directly with the construction industry to improve safety.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: DOB is also dedicated to protecting tenants across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: In addition to our complaint-based and proactive enforcement work, in 2025, our Office of the Tenant Advocate received 1,579 public inquiries,

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: conducted 487 inspections, and made 829 referrals to other sister and state agencies.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Additionally, DOB was grateful to participate in the mayor's rental ripoff hearings to hear directly from tenants about the issues they are facing in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We are working to address the issues we heard during those hearings, including those regarding prolonged or persistent elevator outages, and look forward to working with the council to implement the proposals that require legislative action.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Finally, we are collaborating closely with our partners in HPD, MOPD, and the law department through Fix the City to focus on bad actors who have not come into commission.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: compliance with our enforcement actions and look forward to working on that with you all as well.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: In closing, the Department of Buildings is committed to doing everything within our authority to help address New York City's housing needs while maintaining the highest safety, the highest standard of safety, sustainability, and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: From modernizing our process and technology to strengthening coordination with our sister agencies to improving outreach, DOB is focused on building a system that works.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We are fortunate to have incredible partners in Commissioner Levy and Executive Director Weaver at HPD and MLPT, respectively.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We appreciate the Council's partnership and look forward to continuing to work together.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Sanchez presses on whether the plan's ambitions are backed by sufficient staffing, asking for budgeted vs. actual headcount and vacancy rates for enforcement staff. Levy reports 993 enforcement staff (up 11% in five years) and 353 development staff (up 19%), with 41 new positions allocated. Tagani reports 604 of 650 budgeted DOB inspectors with 25 in pipeline.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions HPD and DOB on staffing capacity and headcount

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask two questions and two topics, and then I'm going to turn it over to my colleagues for their questions before coming back for a second round.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Just so you know, the order in which you have signed up is Councilmember Wilson, Nurse, Public Advocate Williams, and then Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If there's anybody else with questions, please let Austin know.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much for being here today, for all of the work, the big picture, the big level thinking around the housing crisis in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to start with a theme that I've heard in many conversations regarding the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This theme that we started to discuss during the executive budget hearing, that the plan's ambitions are not necessarily backed with the necessary resources to implement them.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We should be aggressively closing high staff vacancy rates in key offices, scaling up staffing overall, investing deeply in core agency functions that don't always make the front page.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But we haven't seen that, particularly in the preservation, the Office of Development, the Preservation Division, the Office of Enforcement and Neighborhood

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Services, Code Enforcement and Litigation Divisions, and within buildings, within the inspectorial units citywide, and especially for the specialized enforcement functions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So there are several commitments.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: that seem to indicate that you all need a lot more staffing to carry these out, the roof-to-cellar inspections, aggressive use of 7A, criminal charges against the worst landlords.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so the first question is around that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So HPD, what is the budgeted headcount of enforcement staff, the actual headcount, and the vacancy rate for fiscal year 26 versus 27?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What increases are you making to the enforcement headcount in order to meet some of these goals?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Sorry, am I on?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So to start, I just want to give a picture of both the development staff and the enforcement staff within the agency.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I know there's always a lot of talk about how much staff do we have and how much staff do we need.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And, of course,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We love getting new staff.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But I do want to point out that right now the total headcount within the enforcement division is 993 staff, which is actually up 11% over the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: On the development side, the staff total is 353, which is up 19% over the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As you know, we were granted significant new staff lines as part of both the housing plan and the speed initiative.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: A total of 41 new positions were allocated to the agency, 24, sorry, 27 for development staff and 14 for our both enforcement and litigation units.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So, yes, I do think we have been given a lot more staff to do the work laid out in the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez raises industry reports of low inspector pay, high turnover, and 70% of inspectors having five or fewer years on the job. Levy reports high morale from office visits and notes pay is negotiated by OLR. Tagani reports average tenure of 6.5 years, says DOB competes with higher-paying private sector, and notes workforce development investments.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions inspector pay, morale, and retention

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to inspector vacancies, we've heard from members in the industry that inspectors themselves are, they're experiencing low morale.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Their pay is low.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's lower than their counterparts, of course, in the private sector.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Turnover is extremely high.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We were told that 70% of inspectors have five years or less on the job.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Please correct.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That if it's incorrect for HPD and the Department of Buildings, this is across NYCHA as well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And that the workloads are increasing over time.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So can you just comment on the pay for inspectors?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there any collective bargaining coming up?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How do we retain this talent that is so key to keeping New York safe?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I'll just speak quickly and then allow Commissioner Tagani to speak.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But I do want to say, and this is more anecdotal than fact, but I have just finished doing a tour of all of our code inspector offices, thanking them for the work they did during the last heat season.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I will just say, you know, both encouraged not only by the morale, which was very high, and again, the work they do is really something to marvel at, but also the tenure of the average person I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And again, I went to all of our offices.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: In some cases, I met folks who have been doing this work for more than 20 years, in some cases as long as 40 years, so I was actually very encouraged.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We do hear the need for additional cars, and we were given an allocation in this year's executive budget for more vehicles to serve those inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As it relates to pay scale, obviously that is negotiated between the Office of Labor Relations and the union, so that is not something squarely within HPD's purview.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But we are very proud of our code enforcement team and feeling like they are also very much up to

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: the challenge and the new initiatives listed in the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: For the DOB side, we have a budget headcount of about 650 inspectors, and currently we have 604 inspectors on payroll with

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: 46 vacancies, but there are 25 inspectors in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The average tenure...

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Based on numbers accumulated earlier this year, was actually higher than five.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: It was about six and a half years for an inspector.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The work that we're doing is certainly, certainly there is a,

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: a high workload.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I will say that similar to Commissioner Levy, going around to the offices, particularly they seem energized by the focus on safety, on tenant protection, the housing plan and messages from the administration seems to have bolstered morale amongst

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: many of the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And I will also say that for the work that we're doing, the difficulties are the same.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We compete against an industry that can pay more.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So we sort of push back by trying to provide workforce development.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We work with the union and get feedback from them and their leadership on what we can do to invest in inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And the last note I'll say on the number is we're actually at our second highest point in many years.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We're going back to 2020 when we were at our highest point.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And so over the last six years, I've really rebuilt and continue to rebuild by filling the vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You're welcome for our advocacy that works.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for precise vacancy rates and whether agencies have enough inspectors for roof-to-cellar inspections and checking every heat complaint. HPD reports 6% vacancy (369 inspectors), DOB reports 7% (46 vacancies with 25 in pipeline). Levy says HPD has sufficient staff for new unit-specific heat inspections starting this heat season.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions vacancy rates and inspector sufficiency for new enforcement initiatives

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But, just kidding.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you both just state what is the vacancy rate now, given the budgeted and actuals?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I think, DOB, you were saying something that's around 7%, but can you both clarify?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And how many vacancies within inspector titles at each agency?

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Right now we're at 7%, but that number will come down once the 25 inspectors in the pipeline come on board.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So as to our code inspectors, we have 369 full-time inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That is a vacancy rate of roughly 6%.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But again, that doesn't include the new hires allocated through the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And do you have, Commissioner Levy, do you have specifics on the average tenure?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I don't have numerical truth other than what I just gave you from anecdotally, but we could certainly get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Caban and Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So follow-up question is how many inspectors do you believe that each of your agencies needs to accomplish the significant expansion of enforcement initiatives, particularly closing every single or

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: checking every heat complaint in a building, for instance, in the roof-to-cellar inspections?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we have been actively preparing for this and again having lots of conversations with the code staff who are very aware of this new protocol.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we do have the staff that we need to be able to do every unit identified inspection as well as the now scheduling for second inspections when failure to gain access occurs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think we are hoping for a warmer winter than last year, but feel ready to take on these new initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And a quick clarification point on process with respect to scheduling inspections.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So it's only scheduling re-inspections, not scheduling the first inspection?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the cross-agency enforcement days concept, how portfolios will be defined and identified. Levy explains the goal is to identify portfolios showing early distress signs and coordinate inspections across agencies and tenant associations. Tagani adds the existing Harassment Task Force complements the new approach.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions cross-agency code enforcement and portfolio approach

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, next question.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The city has committed to a cross-agency approach to code enforcement for problematic portfolios with the mayor's office to protect tenants, providing initial referrals.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: HPD, DOB, and DOHMH will conduct coordinated inspections.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So in the context of this, why take a portfolio-wide approach?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How will portfolios be defined by the agencies and how will they be identified?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think, I believe you're referring to what we were calling enforcement days in the plan, which is really, I think, twofold.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One is when we start to see early signs of distress at a portfolio level, we think it's important that we pay more attention to those buildings early on.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I think we are very focused on coordinating both from an interagency perspective, but also with organized tenant associations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: They obviously are key to getting access to the apartments and to see what's going on inside apartments.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
