utterances.text: So the goal here is really to identify portfolios where we see early signs of distress, get our code enforcement teams out in coordinated effort with each other and also with tenants so that we can sort of

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: get to these portfolios before things deteriorate further.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the administration have a vision?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is it anywhere in the plans to move from enforcement days to more of a holistic approach where this is the way code enforcement takes place versus being reactive?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think it's an addition.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's not instead of, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So our current system is any tenant anywhere in the city can call 311 and have a code inspector come out and inspect their apartment.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think this is just an additional tool into the system.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: on top of the way we currently approach code enforcement, but again with an eye towards getting to certain portfolios early when we're first seeing signs of distress.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I do also just add that the existing platforms like the 10 Harassment Task Force, where DOB, HPD, MOPT, the Attorney General's Office, we continue that

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: as a previous system that complements the new things that we're adding now.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How will you be defining portfolio?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: By portfolio, we just mean owned by a single corporate entity or individual, so multiple buildings affiliated with one ownership.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And how will you know?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Who that owner or single corporate entity is.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'm very good at that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We do, we spend a lot of time piercing corporate veils.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I mean, in some cases it's very obvious because of the registration data that we do get, even though it's still on paper.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We generally know, and when there's work to do to sort of pierce that, we have a data science team within the agency who's able to do it.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There is work involved, so it is not as easy as it should be, but we are generally invariably able to determine who the sort of principal owner is across a portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And with respect to the changes that we're contemplating in today's legislation, Councilmember Banks' property registration, online property registration,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: and I know that in the legislative task force we will be talking about additional changes to help the public have this transparency.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there anything that you have, that you are considering today to define what a portfolio is legislatively?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'm not sure it needs the definition legislatively because generally we just mean an owner who owns multiple buildings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So whether that's five or 15 or 20 buildings, I would call that a portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As it relates to the Councilmember Banks bill for electronic registration, this is something we think is definitely overdue and want to go forward with.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would guess good news, we have already started working to identify a vendor to help us adjust the technology systems that will enable us to do that electronically.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks when each enforcement tool (7A, ERP, criminal charges, COPA, third-party transfer) gets used. Levy explains the layered approach: forcing compliance first, then escalating with litigation, 7A, and new OCA expedited timelines. Tagani discusses jurisdictional strategy between housing court and Supreme Court. Director Weaver adds tenant organization level and financial distress as key factors.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions special enforcement strategy: 7A, ERP, criminal charges, and COPA sequencing

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So moving to special enforcement programs like emergency repair, 7A, the plan lists a number of strategies for being more aggressive for buildings with unsafe conditions, which is a welcome change.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But I think we should drill down on the overall strategy here, specifically what is your explanation for what will be used when.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So how will the various enforcement programs named in the plan fit together into an overall strategy for tenants living in neglected buildings?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the ideal use case?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: for 7A versus when we finish Safer Homes and the Intro 657, the third-party transfer reform, that legislation versus COPA versus criminal charges, when does each program get used?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I'm going to answer and then also give space for Director Weaver to weigh in here.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But generally speaking, our first goal is always to force compliance.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So where we can get an owner to make repairs and do them quickly, that is the ultimate goal.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That said, we are aware that there are some historic small portfolios or individual buildings owned by landlords that have just repeatedly over the years refused to gain compliance.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And sometimes our litigation unit at HPD is bringing cases.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Sometimes DOB is bringing cases.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Sometimes we're both bringing cases.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And so what we are talking about under Fix the City is a really focused effort, which may include things like layering litigation, a 7A on top of an AAP, on top of ERP with DOBs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'll let Commissioner Tagani talk about their legal authority.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But then also working with the law department on new litigation strategies, including some that we think will be very helpful towards pushing for compliance, as well as the initiative

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I talked about earlier in my testimony regarding the agreement we reached with OCA to expedite litigation for these very serious cases.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We do think time is...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: actually the biggest frustration.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I know you've had frustration with vacate orders in your own district where you can just adjourn these cases indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Tenants are literally displaced.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Often HPD is housing them in an emergency shelter.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think these tools sort of layered together with a very clear focus on either finally forcing compliance

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: or where we can't, really pushing to force a change in ownership.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The only thing I will add is that part of the strategy is also figure out where the right jurisdiction is.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So whereas HPD is bringing things in housing court, we work with the law department and maybe bring things in Supreme using criminal summonses and nuisance complaints and maybe team up together.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And then we'll strategize the sequencing of it to make sure that we don't conflict but actually push for change.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Thank you, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And the other two factors that I think we'd consider, in addition to everything that my colleagues have shared, is, one, the level of tenant organization in the building or the portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: We really want to make sure that we are following the lead of people who live in the buildings and pursuing a strategy that works both for the building and for the people who live there.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Secondarily, the level of financial distress in the building and working to sort of smooth the relationship between our enforcement programs and, again, the financial health of the building and really making sure that

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: owners who want to work with the city have access to the preservation tools and owners who are unwilling to comply have access to the preservation tools.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: us to the litigation tools that we know can encourage compliance.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about litigation division staffing (37 attorneys growing to ~40), Partners in Preservation funding ($5 million, 130+ tenant associations formed), and 7A program scale (27 buildings since 2011). Levy says the OCA expedited calendar will significantly enhance 7A capacity and describes exploring ERP alongside 7A to bring more capital into buildings.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions litigation headcount, Partners in Preservation, and 7A expansion

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Lots of court stuff.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Lots of litigation strategy here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So what are the changes that are coming in terms of headcount within the litigation divisions?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So within our HDL, our housing litigation division, we do have new staff as part of the 14 allocated heads that we got as part of the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think the total staff for that division, give me one second, it's in my handy notes, is 39.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, so sorry, 37 attorneys right now, and when we add additional, we'll be closer to 40 attorneys.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But again, we are also finding a lot of collaboration through the legal capacity within the law department, which feels a bit new.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are now meeting, I think,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's probably every other week or twice a month as these three agencies as well as law department to talk about their capacity to enhance our litigation strategies and also to look at new legal strategies,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: some of which aren't quite ready to be discussed publicly, but hopefully will be coming soon.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: We also work really closely with our partners in legal aid, legal services, and the sort of not-for-profit legal community who are important partners in our work.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And that was my next quick follow-up question is partners in preservation and programs to support legal service providers and technical assistance providers and tenant organizers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are those contracts going to be growing or is there going to be increased budget?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In these programs?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I would say Partners in Preservation is very well funded.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's a $5 million program.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're getting to, I think, a year away from the renewal of those contracts.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we've been actually meeting with both the partner agencies and also internally to talk about whether there are any changes to the Partners in Preservation program.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But it has been very successful.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think you saw recently we celebrated the 100th Tenant Association that was formed as a result of that work.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And actually, we're now quite a bit past that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we're closer to 130 tenant associations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we feel very good about that, but I do want to emphasize what Director Weaver just said.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One of the really impressive things about the negotiation we had with the Office of Court Administration is that those expedited calendar timelines apply to cases that we as the city bring or tenants.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So if tenants are represented by Take Root Justice or Legal Services or Legal Aid, those cases will be treated exactly the same way as it relates to the expedited adjudication timeline.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And last leg of...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: of this round for me and then we'll go to colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 7A, what does it mean to supercharge?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So our understanding is from 2011 to present, there have been 27 buildings that have gone through 7A, about 210 units at a capital cost to the city of $2.1 million, which is...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Relatively modest in terms of the work that we, the preservation work that the city does.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So what is the scale of expansion that you are contemplating?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I would say a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One is I think we are somewhat cautious about where we use 7A, mostly because obviously it means that

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There's a temporary marriage or if there's not enough money coming from the rent roll then the 7a administrator isn't really that advantaged One of the things we're contemplating is whether we can use ERP alongside 7a so that there is more capital coming into those buildings

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But I would say more to the point the the again to come back to the OCA adjudicated calendar timeline

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That is actually going to significantly enhance our capacity to bring more cases.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It takes months and months to get a 7A appointed currently because, again, of the ability to just request postponements and adjournments.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So the fact that we will now have this much, much faster calendar will enable us to bring more 7A cases.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have a scale, an intention?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would be loathe to predict an exact number, except to say that I think we're going to be using it very strategically as part of Fix the City, and in cases where every now and again,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: and we find landlords that have virtually abandoned their buildings, I think those are the cases where we really need to use 7A more strategically and more aggressively.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I will now turn it to Councilmember Nurse for her line of questions.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how many preservation deals HPD has made with qualified buyers (Levy estimates 10-20 per year) and what criteria are used to evaluate qualified purchasers. Levy outlines financial capacity, organizational capacity, portfolio conditions, and anti-harassment compliance as key criteria, with annual list refresh.
chapters.title: CM Nurse questions HPD on COPA qualified entities and preservation deal track record

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My questions are mostly just going to front load some of the feedback we've gotten for COPA and have you on the record giving your opinion.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I wanted to talk about the qualified entities.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: As we've heard this bill before, some have called into question HPD's ability to create accountability within a COPA program.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And we know you have worked with preservation buyers and had a list for years with lots of success and with some challenges.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of how many preservation deals HPD has made utilizing entities on the qualified buyers list, even the previous one you had?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'm trying to do the math, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're talking units a lot.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But, you know, we do, I would say, 10 or 20 deals on preservation a year, actually.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Would you say, yeah, close?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, close to 10 or 20 a year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think you are raising a fair point, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are going to need to set out some rulemaking if COPA, we hope it does pass when it passes, both on how we will establish the qualified purchasers list, which will be probably similar to our current preservation analysis, like what we do.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: to determine that somebody is a qualified buyer in our normal preservation programs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We will also need to make sure we have a mechanism to notify the buildings that are going to be subject, and we intend to do that through rulemaking.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then two other issues, establishing penalties for noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And lastly, also notification to tenants, which I think we need to pay a little attention to, is how tenants will be notified when a preservation transaction is actually going forward under COPA.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, that's great.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you for sharing the...

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Like how many deals you're doing per year.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: In the past, you've had the qualified preservation buyers list.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So can you talk about, or maybe those who've had the experience of it, talk about kind of what goes into the qualifications?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: How does one get on that list?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What do they have to show that they can do or have done in the past?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And what might be a process for removing an organization that is, let's say, having too many violations open in their building?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, so generally it's what you would expect in terms of the standards that we look at in creating the current preservation qualified purchaser list.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we're looking at financial capacity.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're looking at organizational capacity.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So are they fully staffed?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Do they have all their proper financial documents, audited financial statements?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're looking at their portfolio across the city, whatever they own and what the conditions in those buildings are.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're looking at compliance with things like anti-harassment laws.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Source of income discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we're looking at like all the factors that would generally lead you to say that this is a qualified, well-capacited buyer.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Because we refresh that every year, if an owner were to, for whatever reason, say start to struggle during the course of a year, we would be reevaluating that in the next year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And it is possible that a group that was on and, you know, currently may fall off in future years.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you're not doing deals with incompetent organizations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are not working with incompetent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Nurse and Sanchez discuss the estimated 2,100 COPA-eligible buildings currently, the shift from one-per-unit violation threshold to a three-plus annual daily average, and why the higher threshold better targets physically distressed buildings at risk of speculation.
chapters.title: CM Nurse questions HPD on COPA-eligible building universe and distress criteria changes

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And just to talk a little bit about the building universe and scope, you know, thanks to a lot of feedback, we've really, really targeted this universe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Using the criteria laid out in the current version of the bill, which includes existing HPD enforcement programs such as AEP, has HPD been able to do an estimate of how many sales would be COPA eligible a year on average?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm going to caveat that it is in fact an estimate.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, same.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So looking across base, the hardest piece of this obviously is just the rolling code violation.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Right, that standard will change constantly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But looking at a moment in time right now, we've arrived at about 2,100 buildings today we think would be eligible under COPA.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And again, we think that number will continue to change primarily because buildings come in and out of our enforcement programs and violations get cleared or accrued.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So that rolling average causes the number to shift.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But I would argue right now about 2,100 buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And even within that, we want buildings that might be COPA eligible, we want them to become ineligible, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So it would be great to...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: To have a good off-ramp for this program as well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The previous version of the bill would have included buildings that had an average of one or more B or C violations per unit at the time of sale.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This criteria, this distress criteria, has been amended to buildings that go on sale with a specific annual daily average.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: From your point of view, can you explain why this change is important?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, I think generally speaking, the one per unit is a very low threshold.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It is, you know, we have a very complicated housing maintenance code.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It is very, very challenging to own a building and, you know, not have any code violations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think the three plus violation count is more reflective of what the intent of the bill is, which is to really capture buildings that are in physical distress and being sold and at risk of, you know, being subject to speculation

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: where it is very critical.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: a preservation purchaser is picking it up to ensure that the building is repaired.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks about funding sources for COPA purchasers. Levy explains HPD cannot finance every deal but PLP, Article 11, and other preservation tools will be available. She describes exploring CDFI partnerships for quick-acting acquisition capital with HPD coming in for a second-stage rehabilitation closing.
chapters.title: CM Nurse questions HPD on COPA funding streams and acquisition timing

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Last two questions, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: One of the other criticisms made against COPA is that housing nonprofits just can't afford to acquire buildings, let alone renovate and maintain them.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So could you talk a little bit about the funding streams?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: COPA purchasers could use, how big those funding pots are.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Also, if you could talk about how long it takes for HPD to approve an acquisition.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if there's any other programs that might complement COPA if implemented.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I really appreciate the question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think what I would say is, first of all, the nonprofit affordable housing community is a fundamental, important partner to HPD.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I do want to say that we have very lucky in New York City to have a huge, huge industry of affordable, not-for-profit housing developers who are critical.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would say it is a fact that HPD cannot guarantee that we will be able to finance every deal that comes online for COPA.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That said, the preservation programs that we currently offer, our PLP program, our Article 11, these are tools that will certainly be available for COPA purchases as they come online.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There will be a question of timing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It is true that we cannot move to, say, a capital loan acquisition very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: while we can move more quickly potentially with the council's support on Article 11.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think we are thinking about two strategies.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One is just the timing and knowing if a building is coming and if it times well with our pipeline, then we will be able to sort of potentially come in in first instance.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The alternative is to think about ways to work with CDFIs and other lenders to establish a capital source.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That nonprofits could access, sort of like our acquisition loan fund in New York City, access that capital for the purposes of acquisition with HPD coming in in sort of a second stage.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's my only questions on COPE.

chapters.summary: Nurse raises the Rent Transparency Act requiring rent stabilization signs in building common areas, showing a copy of the sign and noting it is not very conspicuous. Levy agrees to work on better design and provide data on enforcement actions and 311 complaints about missing signs.
chapters.title: CM Nurse questions HPD on Rent Transparency Act sign enforcement

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I have one last question.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Last year we passed a bill, the Rent Transparency Act.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It forces landlords that have at least one or more rent-stabilized unit to put a sign in the common area.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This is what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's not very conspicuous.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd love to work with you all to make it more conspicuous maybe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But I did have any questions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You might not be prepared to speak on it today given the topic of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But if in the follow-up you could let us know if you've done any enforcement actions, if there have been 311 complaints from tenants who know their building has stabilized units but haven't seen the sign-up.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We have heard from tenant organizers that they've been successful because of some of the signs that tenants realize they're being illegally overcharged for rent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So that's the intent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So, yeah, we'd love to.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Get the sign to look better.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Something.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Maybe some designers.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Well, I didn't design it, so I'm not taking responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't know if there's designers in the sign department.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We would be happy to both work on the design.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Did we design this?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Well, we will be happy to work with you on better design.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't know if it was DOB or HPD, but somebody made it, and it's not as good as it could be.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And Marie says it was us, so it's us.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We will happily make that prettier, and then we will get back to you with the numbers of code inspections or in violations that we've written for noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's why I'm talking about fonts in the safer bill, and text color, because graphics.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Next up, we're going to have Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We're going to have Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, followed by Councilmember Epstein.

chapters.summary: Williams asks why the plan splits evenly between preservation and new production rather than weighting preservation more heavily. Levy explains additional non-capital preservation tools like the tools program supplement the 50-50 capital split. Williams also asks about condo and one-to-two family housing; Levy explains the focus on co-ops due to tax abatement eligibility and affordability targets of 70-120% AMI.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams questions HPD on 50-50 preservation/production split and homeownership affordability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Commissioner Levy, who'd have thunk it 20 years ago?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: One, for the whole administration, I think this is one of the better housing plans I've seen across administrations, so congratulations there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My first question, I always thought, I mean, 50-50 is great, better than we usually do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I've always thought of having a little bit more preservation percentage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to first want to understand why did we go 50-50 and maybe not 60-40, something like that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I mean, I think to your point, public advocate Williams, in years past, right, I think

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I don't think preservation was raised up to an equal level as new production, right, as new construction financing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think we are very pleased that there has been such a great, like, right, we were able to get huge amounts of capital for both preservation and new construction.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think there are some tools that preservation...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Can happen through that don't necessarily just involve capital investment.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So like this tools initiative, which is really meant to stabilize and improve conditions in existing buildings without necessarily having to come in for a tax abatement or a new capital loan.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think while the capital side is, you know, we wanted a balance between new construction and preservation, there's additional things we're trying to do on preservation that aren't just capital specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And with home ownership, I think I saw most of it around condos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm sorry, co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So one, I had a question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is there anything for condos and one and two family homeowners?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And what's the price point for the co-ops and what is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: What is affordable?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: What's our defining affordability?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It is true that we focus very much on affordable cooperatives, less so on condos because they are not eligible for the same tax abatements that co-ops are eligible for.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So to your question of affordability, we typically need an Article 11 or an HDFC to get to an affordable purchase price.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The way we think about affordability in homeownership,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: is through a debt to income ratio.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we're basically looking at what the

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: monthly maintenance needs to be, what taxes and insurance will be, and that sort of backs us into what an affordable mortgage would be.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So combine those four sources, we want to be no more than 30% of the incoming buyer's total monthly income, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And so we're often targeting, it varies somewhere between, I would say, 70% at the low end to 120% AMI at the high end.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Usually we're trying to get closer to an 80% affordability.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So you want those monthly expenses to be no more than 30% of 80% of the monthly income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And is there anything for condo one to families or is it too difficult?

chapters.summary: Williams asks about NYCHA management reform alongside PACT/RAD conversions. Director Weaver describes a new $20 million critical repairs initiative modeled after the Omnibus Call Center and continued oversight of PACT buildings. Williams also shares observations from Syracuse on using code enforcement for public safety, which Tagani expresses interest in discussing further.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams questions administration on NYCHA management and Syracuse code enforcement model

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I mean,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I was working a lot on this in my previous job and had some good successes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I will say one to two families, while have a certain appropriate role to play in our market, they're challenging because of the need for so much.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: You know, development, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The density that we need to achieve is hard to achieve with one to two family homes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That said, there are some neighborhoods that are appropriate and we are actively exploring where we can bring some of the offsite construction models into New York City because of the price points we were able to achieve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Madam Chair, I have one question and a comment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So the question is for both of you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's just about NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is there anything in the plan to deal with the management that is there now and in management when we're trying to do RAD and PAC?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Rad Pack or anything like that to make sure the management is better than it is now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And the comment, which you're happy to respond to, but it's for Commissioner Tagani.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I was recently in Syracuse, met with the mayor, the administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm actually going to cities to try and see what they're doing about public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And it was interesting because they're using code enforcement to address public safety issues, which I thought was pretty unique.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I don't know if we've done things like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd love to speak to you about what I saw there, even off record, but I just wanted to bring that up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yeah, I can speak to the NYCHA question.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: So supporting NYCHA and NYCHA's residents is, of course, a major priority for our administration, and we're really laser-focused on committing billions of dollars to improving public housing quality for NYCHA residents.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Really proud to launch in the housing plan a $20 million critical repairs initiative, which is really modeled after the success of the Omnibus Call Center.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: It's $7.5 million in new funds per year for FY27, 28, and then $2.5 million a year after that.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And its goal is to dramatically increase the number of repair categories eligible for this OCC-style support, where there's a third party that NYCHA residents can call to ensure that they're going to actually get their issues addressed.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: We are very committed to continuing oversight of public housing after it goes through the PACT program.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: So we still believe that those...

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: buildings are public housing and are within the NYCHA family and want to continue to make sure that NYCHA residents, whether they are in a packed building, whether they are in a Section 9 building, have access to the public sector stewardship that public housing can provide.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I would love to talk to you about the public safety conversation that you had.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I will just say that part of the reason why DOB's presence focused on construction safety and safety overall as part of the housing plan does feel different.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I've also been around for a couple of housing plans.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And to see it so anchored, actually seeing the Committee on Construction Safety, part of the overall housing plan is a testament to how we see that as a public safety benefit.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Also, the maintenance and how the streetscape looks, appeals, feels is a problem that DOB has a responsibility to address.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Sidewalk sheds is the thing that I think comes up often for many people from a public safety perspective.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So working to reduce the frequency of it, the longevity of it, making sure that we have a process that asks people to tell us what they're doing to limit the need for it and not just renew it.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: These are some of the things that we're looking at from public safety, but I want to talk more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They had an even different angle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They had an even different angle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'd love to talk to you about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Sia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I'd obviously love to keep talking about some of the concerns that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Manish.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Public Advocate.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Now, Councilmember Epstein, followed by Caban.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether HPD has enough Article 11 funding for the plan. Levy says HPD was granted significant authority, is using Article 11 strategically as a bridge for acquisition with later rehabilitation, and generally targets buildings within statutory Article 11 income limits without seeing AMI as a barrier.
chapters.title: CM Epstein questions HPD on Article 11 resources and AMI structure

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Commissioner Levy, you mentioned Article 11 a lot, and what I've heard this year is, you know, I had a lot of buildings who wanted to get Article 11.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They didn't have enough Article 11 dollars.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you feel like HPD has enough resources related to Article 11 to kind of do the...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Plan you have?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we were very thoughtful coming into the housing plan and the executive budget about how we would use and how much Article 11 we would need.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And we have been granted quite a bit of authority there.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As you know, we're working on a number of preservation deals that are going to be highly reliant on getting those Article 11s.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And again, as we were discussing for COPA, we're starting to sort of see Article 11 as a great bridge for acquisition with then time for us to work through a capital investment for the second phase, which would be rehabilitation, both stabilizing and full rehab.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I do feel like we are using Article 11 very strategically now, and we'll need to do so going forward as we work towards preservation of some of the buildings that I talked about that are both in foreclosure and in bankruptcy.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And some of these developments or some of these buildings have, you know, a variety of income levels in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So how are you going to deal with Article 11 if you have higher AMIs in some of these properties?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Have you looked at changing the structure for AMIs for Article 11?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So generally in the buildings that we're approaching,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We know that they are within the statutory limits of what Article 11 allows.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I can't think of maybe one case I can think of.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I've only been here eight months, but one case I can think of where there was questions in our own mind about whether the building's residents were, frankly, over income to support an Article 11.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Generally, we're trying to target those areas where we have low-cost housing and lower-income tenants.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I, to date, don't think we've seen it as a barrier for preservation.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about increasing housing distress and tenant organizing. Director Weaver emphasizes tenant associations as a key tool and the Enforcement Days initiative requiring tenants to raise issues with landlords first. Tagani discusses the existing building code update going into effect July 2026 and DOB's education efforts. Epstein also asks about the 467-M conversion pipeline timeline, which Tagani says is being tracked effectively.
chapters.title: CM Epstein questions on distressed housing trends, building code, and office conversions

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Director Weaver, we've seen a lot of increase in distressed housing in the city, and I'm wondering what you're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I've seen it in my district, of course, but we're seeing it around the city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And do you feel like there's a pathway through education organizing to get more of these properties in through COPA or through some of these article elements with preservation purchasers based on the increase in distress?

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think it's really important.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: We thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: We know that one of the top tools that tenants can use to ensure that their housing is high quality is to form a tenant association in their building.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And we really want to encourage tenants to come together to form a tenant association and to speak directly to the landlord about the issues that they are facing in their building.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: In our Enforcement Days initiative, which we're hoping to roll out soon, we are looking to make sure that tenants have actually tried to raise issues with landlords first before they come to the city.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yes, there is issues with the stress in our building and we also in our buildings and we also need to make sure that tenants are calling the landlord notifying them and

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And working together with each other to try to get repairs made and then calling the city if that doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But you've seen an increase in involvement there, an increase in distress, an increase in tenants reaching out.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Have you seen that kind of transition?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Well, you've been only, it's been six months, so, I mean, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you've noticed that, too, and through your work now.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: You know, we work with tenant associations every single day who are reaching out to us to try to ensure that they can get repairs in their building, and we look to continue to do that work, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The only thing I'd add here is from the DOB perspective, when you have tenants who are looking to have repairs done, or you have owners who are themselves going through extensive rehabilitation for a long time, trying to work within the building code specifically was difficult.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And so at the end of last year, we passed existing building code.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: It goes into...

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Deployment implementation in July of next year, and we've been spending the last year into next year trying to educate people.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Basically, I'm saying that DOB has its own responsibility to make sure that people who are trying to do the right thing have the tools to do it and the education to do it.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So whether it's a tenant or owner, we hope the existing building code, the changes, and the streamlining will help.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And Commissioner Degani, I'm just wondering about the, we've seen an increase in conversions going through DOB from commercial to residential.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you feel like the deadline to the pipeline that Albany's put forward is giving enough timeline for some of these conversions to happen?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you feel like they need to be extended?

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: You know, I think we've actually worked very closely with the

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Division of Housing Assistance at HPD for the tax abatement projects.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: But as we know, the project pipeline for office residential conversion is much larger and has been around for decades.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So there's 17,000 units between 1995 and 2007 alone in lower Manhattan using those tools.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And so we've had a lot of experience.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We do think that the process we have set up to work through the different deadlines for 467M is working.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We're tracking our information together.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And especially those projects that go through the major project program at DOB, which is

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: a particular pipeline that works with complex projects, assigns a project manager that actually works before filing and gives them a dedicated person to walk them through the entire process.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Those projects have been the most successful, so we're working to get the word out about that.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And actually, that's one of the areas that speed grew by investing seven additional staff members since we saw so much success, particularly with office residential conversion.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about ADU progress and whether state legislative changes are needed. Levy reports 27 ADU applicants in pipeline with 17 more expected, noting challenges with pre-development work for homeowners. Tagani reports 261 applications under Local Law 27, with 48% for basement/cellar conversions, and says rules for manufactured ADUs and amnesty should be finalized by year-end.
chapters.title: CM Epstein questions on ADU and basement legalization pipeline

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Chair, if I can just get another quick minute.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I just want to talk to you about the ADUs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know you mentioned how many ADUs have been developed now over the last year.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you think we need to go back to Albany to either expand?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Expand the pilot project or to extend the timeline of the pilot?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, so I just want to make a distinction between ADUs and the basement legalization, which is the pilot.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The Plus One program, which is the ADU program, is actually starting to really, I think, gain momentum.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: challenging because the pre-development work that goes into designing the ADU, determining if there's enough space for a standalone unit, or whether it needs to be a conversion of an existing structure, takes time and actually resources and you need an architect, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So it's not really about code, it's just about

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: limited space.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We have about 27 ADU applicants in the pipeline right now moving forward and another 17 right behind them that we expect to enter the pipeline shortly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We would like to keep moving that and again I think it's a question of making sure we have the right supports through our nonprofit partners for the pre, I would almost call it the pre-pre-development phase of the ADU development.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, one is, do you think that the strict kind of structures, not allowing more products to go forward, is there something we need to be doing differently on the state level to increase the flow of basements and ADUs?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I mean, to be honest, I ran the ADU program for the state, and we found this to be challenging everywhere, including places where land is not so constrained or space, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think it's just a challenging thing in a very dense place like New York City.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That said, the amount of interest is overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's really exciting.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And the fact that we now have resources with which to finance that, along with the state resources, I think it's really not a legislative solution.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we need to just keep pushing hard on the front end for that pre-development phase.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: More broadly under the local law.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: 27 piece, we actually have about 261 applications in.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Almost half, 48% or 126, are for basement and cellar conversion.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So we're seeing, to the commissioner's point, because of the constraint of land, we're really seeing attic, basement, cellar as being a main place where people are looking to deploy this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I just want to shout out the ADU4U tool.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's really nice looking at it last night.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Did not work for my address, so I will be following up with you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I do want to know if I can have an ADU in my basement.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Couldn't see that last night.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But just since you mentioned the existing building code, Commissioner Tagani, you know, the kind of, that kind of guidance that the city is providing through ADU for you would be beautiful to see, you know, especially for small homeowners who, you know.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Experience the city as a Byzantine regulator, it would be really helpful to, you know, if we can adapt that kind of guidance for small homes.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So we've got a dedicated website.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We actually have a monthly newsletter.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Sirakis has a crossword puzzle that he includes for those who want a game to understand more about the existing building code.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We've been signing up and doing seminars, webinars with different industry partners, and we'll continue to build out the website and those tools.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We also...

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: have implemented in our monthly industry meetings and our open webinar, our monthly online meetings with property owners and license reps.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So always open to do more, and especially if you want to convene property owners, we'd love to work with the council on that as well.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We're very focused on getting the word out about this.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great, excellent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over now to Councilmember Caban, followed by Riley, and then Joseph.

chapters.summary: Caban asks about the Our Home program for converting rental buildings to cooperatives, whether COPA-eligible buildings could use Our Home funding, and what financing combinations are available. Levy explains Our Home targets 10-40 unit buildings, recommends COPA buildings work with a sponsor for stabilization before conversion, and confirms multiple financing tools (PLP, Article 11, Neighborhood Pillars) could be combined.
chapters.title: CM Caban questions HPD on Our Home program and COPA financing options

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I just have a few questions focused on financing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The block-by-block plan, it mentions a new program called Our Home that's supposed to facilitate the conversion of rental buildings into resident-controlled cooperatives.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so, I mean, to start, I just want to know what would be eligible for the Our Home program and would a qualified preservation buyer be able to purchase a COPA-eligible building with Our Home funding?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if so, then how would that work?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So the program is right now intended for, I guess I would say, two categories of buildings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So those would be privately owned, typically rent-stabilized buildings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're looking at projects that are probably somewhere between 10 and 40 units as like the kind of sweet spot that we haven't put a hard line on that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So rent-stabilized buildings where they wanted to go through a conversion and become owners is one categorical.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then I would say even within our own portfolio of rental buildings that are of that size, we would certainly entertain a conversion using our home.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: What was the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Oh, that would a qualified preservation buyer be able to purchase through COPA?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Though I do want to say, just years ago I worked for a nonprofit called YouHave, and one of the great lessons there is it is very challenging to go through a conversion from rental to collective ownership while there is physical distress, particularly deep physical distress.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So one of the things we would likely advocate for as the COPA buildings were to come through, because they are by definition going to be distressed, that they work with a sponsor in the first instance to

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: help them get through stabilization, renovation, and then a conversion could come on the back end of that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Will the new program provide acquisition funding, rehab funding, a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's for both.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It will both be for the acquisition and then the renovation of the building where that's necessary, when it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And would they be able to use this and another program, for example, like Neighborhood Pillars?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Would Neighborhood Pillars be a place where there could be acquisition and renovation to a COPA-eligible building?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Pillars is not intended necessarily for conversion to collective ownership.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So, right, we both could be tools for financing the acquisitions that may...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Materialized through COPA as well as other programs including our participating loan program.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Again, we could use Article 11 potentially as a standalone source depending on the depth of physical distress in the building.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think all of the tools that we have for acquisition and rehab will be made available as part of the COPA financing tools.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It will come down, as I said,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: earlier to timing and just the availability of the resources, but we do expect to use all of the tools in our toolbox.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, guys.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Oh, within the time limit.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Kavanaugh.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Riley.

chapters.summary: Riley asks whether HPD has sufficient bond cap for ambitious production goals. Levy cites the 25% test change and significant capital commitments. Riley then raises delays in HPD project manager assignment for HDFCs aging out of regulatory agreements. Levy discusses the expiring DAMP tax cap affecting ~1,000 HDFC co-ops and ~250 under HPD regulatory agreement, offering to follow up on specific sticking points.
chapters.title: CM Riley questions HPD on bond cap, project manager delays, and HDFC expirations

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So good morning to Commissioner Tajani, Commissioner Levy, and Director Weaver and your team.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you so much for testifying with us here today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So we often hear from different stakeholders about the lack of funding in HPD's budget that leads to delays in receiving subsidies during HPD's June and December closing windows.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: With an ambitious housing plan being set by this administration to develop hundreds of thousands of housing units, which the council believe is needed as well, included heavily subsidized affordable housing unit.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Does HPD have the bond cap necessary to achieve this goal?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As you know, I think it was last year, maybe two years ago, right, there was a major significant change to the tax credit program.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's called the 25% test.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So the test was lowered from 50% to 25%.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That became a hugely important tool for us in terms of extending the capacity to finance both 4% and 9% deals.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So that has been hugely helpful.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then the commitment that was made in terms of capital, which we use along.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: side, the 4% and the 9% for the next two years, as you know, is a huge amount of resources that will make sure we don't leave any of that bond cap on the table.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Furthermore, before projects even get off the ground, we are hearing that some of the same stakeholders about delays and being assigned the HPD project manager, particularly amongst those for the HDFCs who are aging out of their regulatory agreement.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And are seeking a new Article 11.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Given these delays and the target of developing upwards to 700,000 units of housing within the next 10-year span, does HPD have the necessary headcount to handle these proposals?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd actually love to follow up with you more about exactly what portion of which HDFCs you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There are two things happening right now.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One is the expiration of the damp tax cap.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So there are about 1,000 HDFC co-ops in the city that benefit from the tax cap, and we know that it's expiring.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And so we are certainly having conversations with our...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: You know, partners in the state about the need to renew that, that damn tax cap, which is critical to the affordability of these HDFCs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There's then another about 250 HDFC co-ops that are actually under regulatory agreement with HPD.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So if there are issues there in terms of, you know, those that are going to the end of their article 11, or they need to renew that, or they just need a capital loan,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would love to talk with you more about where there is sticking points.

chapters.summary: Riley questions how HPD will work with City Planning to plan for hundreds of thousands of units in already dense neighborhoods, and how to protect existing Black and Brown residents from displacement. Levy acknowledges the 700,000 figure is aspirational, with HPD committing to 200,000 over 10 years, mentions two rezoning plans and micro-neighborhood plans, and points to the strategic equity framework's anti-displacement section.
chapters.title: CM Riley questions HPD on 700,000 unit goal, neighborhood plans, and anti-displacement

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next question is, the city of New York has not produced 700,000 units of housing since like 1920s, which was a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How will HPD work with the Department of City Planning to adequately plan for the infusion of hundreds of thousands of units of housing in neighborhoods that are already densely populated and lacking critical infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So point is well taken.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We understand that, you know, the draft report we put out regarding what the growth targets need to be for the city are very aspirational.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: HPD obviously is not committing to financing 700 units, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So our commitment here is 200,000 units of new housing over the next 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We do, as we've talked about, have a big commitment of new staff and a very big commitment of new capital, particularly for the next two fiscal years, which we see as a big down payment

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: towards moving in the direction of that ultimate goal of 200,000 units with the commitment right now to build 28,000 units over the next two years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We understand that some neighborhoods will be more challenged in terms of building, but we do want to be frank about what we need.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then we want to be collaborative with every council member and every community board in every district to figure out how to try to meet those aspirational goals.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Will you guys be announcing any future neighborhood plans to possibly achieve those goals?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There are two.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Rezoning plans right now that are being...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: One in my district, I think.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, so two that you know about being considered.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then I think...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We are, one of the things named in the housing plan are these sort of micro-neighborhood plans, which are not as big as like full-wide community rezonings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
