utterances.text: And I think we are anxious to start to move that, especially for the reason you point out, which is that we have really high aspirational goals for the amount of housing we need to build as a city.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Chair, just one more question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Being tasked with creating development opportunities, and you mentioned the White Plains Road Neighborhood Plan, which is in my district.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: For all these potential units, how will HPD, along with sister agencies, work to protect existing black and brown New Yorkers and communities like mine in the Northeast Bronx, as we're talking about a lot of housing production,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: worried about rising rents, worried about displacements.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We have a lot of residential units within my household as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So, Commissioner, we could definitely speak about this after this, but those are concerns that my community, communities in Southeast Queens, are having when we're talking about this development that's coming.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I just want to say we completely understand and share some of those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: You all noticed the part of the draft proposal that was put out in the strategic equity framework, which is sort of the third section.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There is a whole section just dedicated to stabilizing neighborhoods, which is very much about anti-displacement strategies.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So this is very much on our mind as well as our fair housing goals.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I'm happy to follow up and talk about what type of anti-displacement strategies we need to be sure.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just want to continue being a partner with you guys.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So thank you so much for.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'm testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Joseph.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how council members can hold qualified entities accountable and about private financing capacity for COPA. Levy explains the annual list refresh process and describes CDFI partnerships (CPC, Enterprise) as potential acquisition capital sources. Joseph also asks about renovation timelines; Levy estimates ~18 months from construction loan closing to completion, with relocation plans required before starting.
chapters.title: CM Joseph questions HPD on COPA accountability, financing, and renovation timelines

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Happy to see you all.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Excited about Prospect Park South rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Very excited.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Community is excited.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: As we talk about making sure that we're keeping our communities in place, we also have to hold bad actors and bad landlords accountable.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And you've seen in my district, you came for a walkthrough, you see the dilapidated conditions that my community is in.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I'm looking forward to see how we can escalate and move those complaints forward.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But today my question is, and some of those buildings we walk through could benefit from a COPA, right?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I would love to see where we can, you know, meet halfway.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But my few questions is, what is the role of the council member, if any, in the process of holding qualified entities on the preservation buyers list accountable?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do we do that?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question is how would the council members also hold those?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how would you, how does the entities on the preservation by list, how are they held accountable?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So as we sort of discussed earlier, the list will be in, like, when the bill passes, like the first list would be issued based on the criteria I outlined, but then we will revisit that list every year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So it is not just because you get on once you automatically stay on.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Obviously, these are nonprofits, and so, you know, we feel confident that we'll be working primarily with mission-based organizations, but that isn't to say that they don't.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Sometimes turn the wrong corner.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we will refresh that list every year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And if we find that there's an owner who's fallen out of compliance or into financial instability, right, they would no longer be included in future lists.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then we would also work to make sure any buildings that they have already acquired through COPA are addressed either through code enforcement or through our preservation initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What kind of private financing to pair with HPD acquisition and preservation tools?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What is their lending capacity for COPA eligible building acquisition?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we got to talk money.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We do have to talk money.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So as I said, I think there is going to need to be some private-public partnership here to make COPA truly effective.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So one of the things we've been talking about is gathering all of the different partners we have at CDFIs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So CPC is a good example.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Enterprise is a good example.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So these are entities that also finance affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think having a sort of version of the acquisition loan fund, which was meant to be exactly this, quick acting capital that responsible landlords can use to acquire projects,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: even if that means we would do a second stage closing with HPD specifically around renovation, I think that will be critical to expanding the capacity under COPWA.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And those buildings we've seen in dilapidated conditions, is there a timeline as to what the renovations would look like?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's a very good question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: You know, it depends on the depth of distress, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So sometimes we're doing what we call like a moderate rehab.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Other times we're doing a substantial rehab.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Other times still a gut rehab.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So hopefully we're not in that third category very often and we're getting to the buildings before it turns into that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would say on average from the time we close a construction loan to the time we complete a rehab scope is usually around 18 months, sometimes a little faster, sometimes a little faster.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And is there a plan if you do move out the tenants as to where they will be placed and upon?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Well, we don't start, yes, we don't start renovations if relocation is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Optimally, you would not have to move tenants out at all, or alternatively, you might have the ability to checkerboard if there's enough vacancies in a building, meaning they don't actually have to leave the building, just perhaps their unit.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But we don't start renovations until we've identified acceptable relocation options.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Anybody for a second round?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Here we go.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: My favorite part where I just ask forever.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No, I'm kidding.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Those who...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: who are going to be testifying, I will be brief so that you can testify.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes only ~44 ADU units in pipeline versus City of Yes projections of 1,800 per year. Levy explains the pre-development challenges for homeowners and explores manufactured ADU models. Tagani says rules for manufactured ADUs and amnesty/ATR program should be finalized by year-end, and notes LPC released its ADU map in June.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: ADU rollout numbers and scaling challenges

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so the first question I want to ask is just a quick follow-up on the ADU conversation.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So you said between the Plus One program and the basement legalization pilot, there are under 50 conversions or ADU units in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes, it's about 27 plus 17.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just thinking back to City of Yes for housing opportunity and the proposal, the projections were that there would be 82,000 units created over 15 years, which puts us at about

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 27,000, or excuse me, puts us at about 1,800 units per year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so how do we get there?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How does the administration?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, I think as the program, and I'll let Commissioner Dugani add to this, but I think as, and again, you know, I was working more on this from the state's perspective, but I think the challenges are the same.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It really is the amount of work that has to happen at the front end.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And keep in mind, right, like homeowners are taking this on directly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So they're not necessarily experienced at construction.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: They don't have architect rights.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So there is just a tremendous amount of work to kind of get the right team together to do the analysis.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Is it going to be an extension to the home?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Is it going to be conversion of existing?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Ancillary structures or is it going to be a standalone unit?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One of the things we're exploring

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: for where those standalone units may work is a manufactured ADU model.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we've issued an RFP recently to solicit that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And the reason for that is that they can be built and delivered much, much faster than a stick-built unit.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So one of the strategies we're looking at is off-site construction ADUs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But again, those will only work primarily where there's room for a standalone ADU unit.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think for the rest of, I would say, two-thirds of the ADU population that we're talking to, we're just going to need to keep adding technical assistance and support for that early pre-development work.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I do see the program picking up.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're not quite where we need to be, but I think we're going to have to sort of keep adding upfront resources so that homeowners can move through the process more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Well, just picking up on the last element for the manufactured construction piece, DOB's responsibility will be to craft the rules and make sure there's clarity.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Again, like every other step that we've taken, whether it was the state changes in 2024, City of Yes,

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: the rules are necessary to give the market, the industry, individual homeowners the clarity that you need to move forward, and that can take time.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So we're working on different parts of the ADU program or conversion program.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The amnesty program or the ATR program that will give people a pathway to legalization will also be a major driver to get

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: giving people predictability and bring folks into the legalization world.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And we expect those rules to be finalized and be available by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So those are two pieces of clarification that should inject more energy into this work and allow us to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's helpful.

chapters.summary: Sanchez raises that one-third of evictions were in affordable housing buildings and questions the tools program's response to the 70% one-shot deal denial rate. Levy describes tools as upstream intervention including clearing back rent through grants/loans to free capital for better management. Director Weaver adds the tenant support helpline fielded 21,000 calls last year.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: stabilizing aging affordable housing and tools program

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so this is the second bucket of question here is around the plan, what the plan says and does not say around stabilizing the aging affordable housing stock that low-income New Yorkers rely on.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So, you know, fully...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Let me pull up the right note.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Fully one-third of evictions in the previous year were at affordable housing projects or affordable housing buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And with respect to what the plan says about stabilizing this portfolio or these properties, you indicate the tools program.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so the first question here is with respect to the tools program, there are various components.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But one of the pieces of feedback that we have received time and again from the industry and from housers is that you know

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: the, I can't find the notes, so I'm just doing this from memory, is that the, oh my gosh, my brain is blanking.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The one-shot deal program has had, it has a 70% denial rate.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So how do you square that away with the expansion of the tools program and stopping evictions before they start?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would just say, and I think both I and Director Reaver want to comment on this, I think tools is intended to work with existing property

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: subsidized, HPD subsidized property owners early in the process at getting access to tools that are already available to them, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Again, so not having to go through a new application for Article 11 or a new application for financing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: One of the things we're talking about as part of tools is how to get upstream in the process so that we're not relying so heavily on one shots, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And so I want to be frank that we have not fully figured out exactly what to do or why we are seeing so much fragility in terms of rent collection.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But what we have heard pretty consistently is that better asset management and better services, wraparound services at the building level has improved rent collection a lot.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So one of the things we're exploring with tools is if we can help clear back rent through a grant or a loan from HPD to the property owner

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: in order to then free up capital, which would otherwise go to legal expenses, to bring in better management, better wraparound services, we think that will have a stabilizing effect.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we've included in the tools outline a pilot to sort of test certain versions of that to see if it does actually make a difference in terms of both stabilizing the cash flow and help more residents get current and stay current on their rent.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: I would just add that the city's public engagement unit runs a tenant support helpline that has been tremendously helpful at actually workshopping one-shot deal applications with renters so that their one-shot deal applications are successful.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: They fielded more than 21,000 calls last year, and they continue to be a really critical resource that the mayor's office for tech tenants works closely with to ensure that people are getting access to tools to help pay their background if that's what is needed.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And Director Weaver, what are the most common reasons for these rejections?

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you on that, but the applications are complicated, they are long, and we are looking for ways to really support people in making sure that they're filling out the application to the best of their ability so that their application is successful.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And tools writ large, have you already launched the program?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How much funding has been allocated to each aspect of tools?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And how many buildings do you expect to work with in the first year?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we have launched.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: In the first stage, we spent a lot of time training our asset and property management staff on the new protocols around requests for reserves.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Expanded tax abatements under 420C.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So that was phase one.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Phase two was a series of roundtables that we held with groups like NYSAFA and A&HD and the housing conference to make sure folks know about the program and also to take feedback.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We didn't want to sort of roll it out without getting some input from our partners on what they thought would be most

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: helpful.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Now we're at the stage where we've onboarded the three technical assistance providers, Enterprise LISC and the Housing Partnership, and we've sort of just sort of figured out amongst ourselves who will be serving which organizations that are interested in that additional technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And lastly, we're now engaged with about half a dozen individual developers on their actual portfolios who are working to take advantage of one or more of the different options under tools.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how many LiTECH properties lack 420C abatements. Levy says HPD is analyzing the universe and will follow up. Sanchez then asks about tools for Mitchell-Lamas and HDFCs. Levy acknowledges this is a missing piece, describes plans for new contracts with co-op specialists like UHAB, and discusses different strategies needed for Mitchell-Lamas versus HPD-subsidized stock.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: 420C tax abatement and Mitchell-Lama tools expansion

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Talking about a 420C, I always thought it was as a right if you were a LITECH, or not as a right, but it went along with every LITECH deal.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So could you tell us how many LITECH properties do not have a 420C and what scale you would anticipate to reach with 420C?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, just to be frank, I would want to get back to you with an estimate for that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we were a little surprised, too, that this was sort of a tax abatement that was available that hadn't been fully utilized by some of our partners.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we've started to do some analysis.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: My colleague Adam, my first deputy commissioner, has been really sort of digging in on what is the universe and how do we match it up to the groups that we're hearing from directly who are interested in tools.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But if you'll allow it, I'll have to get back to you with a projection on what is the total universe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Make a note here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then with respect to tools again, and specifically the eviction prevention side of it, bringing into the public a conversation that you and I started, Commissioner,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: the use of tools for Mitchell-Lamas or HDFCs.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have an update for us in terms of helping to stabilize those properties?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: It's not much different than the update we just exchanged last week.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But generally speaking, we agree that that is actually a missing piece for the Mitchell-Lama, particularly co-ops, but not exclusively.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So for the reasons we discussed, you know, co-ops require a specialized type of assistance that is really, I think, best put forward by groups like UHAB, possibly others like Habitat, who really specialized in that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think, and that's not to say that Enterprise and LISC and the Housing Partnership couldn't also provide that technical assistance, but I think we're looking specifically at expanding the TA providers for a tool-type program for Mitchell-Lama

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: that would include groups like UHAB, and there's another organization that we're talking to who I think really has an understanding of the asset management challenges that Mitchell-Lamas are going through.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: They're a little different than the existing HPD subsidized stock.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: They don't tend to have these reserves, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And they have different– an Article 2 is different than an Article 11.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So there's probably a different– universe of strategies that we need to deploy for Mitchell Lama.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But to be frank, your point was well taken when you raised it for Kingsbridge.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I think we are now looking to see if we can come up with a comparable early upstream intervention to help Mitchell Lamas.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Many of them we know are going to need a big capital investment and we're prepared to make those investments.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But I think

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think these are good strategies to deploy on the way.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So would you anticipate that there are going to be additional contracts with those technical assistance providers?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I do think we will need new contracts to bring on the co-op specialists.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: With respect to the loans that are described in that tool section, why would an owner take advantage of a city loan for operating expenses if they have no guarantee that new revenue would come to pay back that loan?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So are we talking about a preservation loan?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The tool section makes mention of making more financing available to these owners.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Why would they take advantage of more financing if they are worried about collecting?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, well, generally, if we're talking about capital investment financing, and they're coming in because they have deferred capital needs and they need to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And obviously, HPD, when we're financing a project, is on very, very favorable terms, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Often no or low interest with, you know, flexibility on term.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we certainly wouldn't advise that any of our not-for-profit partners recapitalize unless it's necessary and unless we can see that the cash flow will be sufficient to pay back those loans.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But I would say tools isn't primarily as focused on making capital loans as...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: it is on accessing existing resources, including their own building reserves, and having flexibility with those reserves to look across their own portfolio,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: and also to just frankly to make it not so challenging to work with, you know, it takes frankly too long for HPD to receive those requests, process those requests, so part of the tools initiative is to say this should take no more than 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the insurance program scale and market impact. Levy targets 20,000 units insured by end of 2027 and 100,000 by 2030, expecting competitive pressure to drive down market premiums. On water assistance, Levy defers to DEP but notes plans to serve 75,000 residents next year, up from 50,000.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: city-backed insurance program and water assistance

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, with respect to the city-backed insurance program and water assistance programs, but starting with the insurance program, so the plan talks about $100 million over three years.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You mentioned in your opener that you have received 22 responses to the RFEI.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you talk to us about the scale of this program, how many buildings you are hoping to reach within the first year, two, five?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And what the goal is of the administration with respect to an impact on the insurance market or anything else?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What do you anticipate will come for this outside of the buildings that directly benefit?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it's an excellent question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think the first is to just reiterate what we've said publicly and what we are committed to, which is working to, once we have the partner and the program is operational,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: it's hard to say number of buildings because we're targeting a unit count, so it really depends how big or small the buildings that join.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The program will be, but the goal is to get to 20,000 units insured by the end of next year.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So that would be the end of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then 100,000 units by the end of 2030.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We do expect to see, once we get to scale like that, we will be helping to drive, hopefully, the competitive market downward, which is really critical.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we do think an ancillary benefit of this is if we're offering affordable insurance premiums through this new city-backed initiative, other providers will have to either match us or beat us, which is what we would like to see.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I will just say this is becoming more and more of a focal point for us.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The insurance premiums are one of, if not the biggest driver of distress amongst both affordable housing providers and privately owned rent-stabilized landlords.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's helpful to hear.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: With respect to the multifamily water assistance program, this is a DEP program, so let me know if you're equipped to respond to it, but timeline and scope of that expansion and which buildings would be prioritized?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I do have to defer since it is not a program run by...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: By HPD, but we are very glad to see the increase in support for this program.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We know it's hugely important and that water bills are also a stressor, both on individual tenants and on building owners.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: What we know from them is I think that they intend to serve 75,000 residents next year, which is up.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: From about 50,000 in past years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So that's a market increase.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And that's targeting affordable properties as well?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think it's an income-based program.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks when the Bronx will feel the Bronx Plan's impact. Director Weaver confirms interagency conversations have begun with MOPT, Mayor's Office of Equity, Deputy Mayor for Community Safety, and NYCHA, with community engagement planned for late fall. Sanchez urges inclusion of the Deputy Mayor for Community Safety.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: Bronx Plan status and interagency coordination

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The Bronx Plan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The plan spotlights the Bronx, and this is much needed and appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And it talks about the all-of-government approach and the potential that it has to move the needle for our folks.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, in previous hearings, including in the executive in May, I talked about the troubling and, you know, alarming trend of the doubling of fires in the Bronx and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We talked about root causes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We talked about what can be done.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So in the context of the myriad challenges facing the Bronx, we'd love to understand the status.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Have interagency conversations internally begun?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: When will the Bronx feel the workings of the Bronx plan?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And just to put in a plug, a major plug, to please, please, please include the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety on the Bronx plan because it's so central to what we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: We actually had a call with the Deputy Mayor for Community Safety on the Bronx Plan this morning at 9.30, so happy to say yes to that question.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yes, interagency conversations have begun on the Bronx Plan, led by HPD, led by HPD.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: but with the Mayor's Office of Equity and Racial Justice, MOPT, and we are, again, bringing in the Deputy Mayor for Community Safety and also NYCHA into this work.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: The goals are to really address building conditions, to address health disparities and support quality of life and public realm improvements.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And we are focused on both highest need areas in the Bronx, but also areas where

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: very many people live in existing affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And so really thinking about ways that we can complement the affordable housing that we are providing in the Bronx with other initiatives like

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: streetscape improvements, like activating ground for retail, working closely with also the Mayor's Office of Early Child Care Education and really thinking about what other needs exist here.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: So looking forward to really continuing to build out that work and to start community engagement sometime in the late fall.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And yes, on the fires as well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Sheds and the Bronx Plan and the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety.

chapters.summary: Sanchez raises sheds as magnets for dangerous activity in her district. Tagani proposes mapping shed addresses, case management with owners, enforcement canvassing, and new rules reducing shed permit duration to 90 days with owner representation requirements. He also discusses Thornton Tomasetti report recommendations for longer inspection cycles for newer buildings.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: sidewalk sheds and public safety in the Bronx

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I won't go into too many of my own local issues, but I've been having probably weekly discussions with the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety, for which I'm very thankful.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: One of the themes that is arising in this hotspot where we've had arson, open-air drug sales, like you name it, it just feels like a part of my community is something out of a movie, is sheds.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Sheds are a place where dangerous activity happens, where the community members do not feel safe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so a question for buildings, a question for you all is, what can I take back and what can communities dealing with sheds that attract negative activities, what can we take back to our communities in terms of how will these sheds be taken down?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What do we do to get them down?

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So I think just coming out of this discussion is working with your team to get a list of all the addresses, start mapping out these sheds.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We can start doing the background research on each of these properties to understand what the source of the shed issue was.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Is it related to a facade inspection report, an individual issue?

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And we've had success engaging with owners to figure out, is it something that we can do from the plan review permitting process?

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Is there a...

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: something that they need or we can connect them with other resources, just start doing that case management to get those sheds down.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: At the same time, our enforcement team will go out as soon as we have addresses to start looking and canvassing these sheds to see if there are any problems with the sheds or the repairs,

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: just to make sure they have the appropriate lighting, that there isn't any structural issues.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We'll do that in parallel.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So we'll evaluate, see if the sheds are...

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Are not up to code, make sure that they are at least working properly and have the appropriate lighting, which hopefully helps with the public safety piece.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And then beyond that, we want to bring the sheds down.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So separate and apart from new rules that will go into place that now bring down the permitting process, permitting allowance for one year to 90 days, the new requirements for owners to represent to us through a licensed

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: professional, what they're doing to bring down that shed, that's citywide.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: We will work as part of Bronx Plan to focus on these sheds particularly.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And do you anticipate that some of the changes that you are making described in the speed report described in, I always get it wrong, Thomas, I'm looking at a girl, Thomas, okay, I'm not going to remember the name of the report.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Thornton Tomasetti.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thornton Tomasetti, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That one.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's sweet.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That report.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: The beloved TT, yes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The Get Shuts Down report, the technical report.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Some of the changes included...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: you know, differential treatment for newer properties, the longer cycles between local law 11 inspections, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you anticipate those changes will help the Bronx in particular with respect to the number of sheds we have up?

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I think parts of the Bronx where there is newer construction will see the benefit of the fact that our analysis showed that buildings, particularly in this situation, 40 years or newer,

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: if they have a safe report, can extend to 12 years before they have another full inspection using abbreviated visual inspections in between.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Parts of the borough where the older building stock exists, we are moving from five to six years because we can create a little bit more breathing room but still maintain that safety.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And then where there are campuses that require sheds to be erected, trying to reduce the radius of those sheds so that it's not completely consuming

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: the sidewalk and the areas of walkway, returns more space to people, and also is less cost for less shed to have to go up.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: So, yes, I think different parts of the Bronx will see it impact them positively differently.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez questions the 57,000 vacant rent-stabilized units reported by HCR and why the Unlocking Doors program failed. Levy cautions against overstating warehoused units, notes the Housing Vacancy Survey will provide better data, and says J51 reauthorization will be a major tool for bringing vacant units back online.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: rent-stabilized vacancies and Unlocking Doors program

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, vacancies in rent-stabilized units across the city.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As of April 1st of 2025, the HCR reported more than 57,000 rent-stabilized apartments were vacant, approximately 6% of the overall rent-stabilized universe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That's 15%.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: increase from the previous year, 2024.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: However, in the block-by-block report and the rental ripoff report, the discussion around rent-stabilized vacancies and rent-stabilized buildings really focused on the Unlocking Doors program and how unsuccessful it has been.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so a question here is, what does the city believe is driving the number, the increasing number of vacancies in rent-stabilized units?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Does HPD or the administration believe that there was...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That unlocking doors was structured poorly or what reasons do you ascribe for the reasons for the failure of unlocking doors and

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: any other details that you can share to address this specific universe of low-cost homes?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think we're still trying to diagnose exactly by having conversations with our partners and owners of these rent-stabilized buildings about why unlocking doors

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: did not have better uptake.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But a couple of things I want to say about just the statistic first is that we do know that the vacancy rate in rent-stabilized housing is very, very low.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We're in the middle now of the housing vacancy survey, which kind of digs in much more deeply and will give us a better picture of exactly what the vacancy rate looks like.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I also want to make sure, with all due respect to my colleagues at HCR, that we're

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: aren't misunderstanding the data that they're putting out.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think sometimes these numbers come out and people think these are warehoused units, the same units stay vacant for years.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That's not necessarily the case.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: This is like a moment in time.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So, you know, units may be vacant for any reason, either because we've just completed construction and they're going through lease up or because they're just, you know, gone on to turnover.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I think it's important not to overstate.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: You know, what that number that HR puts out says.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: To your question about why the take-up has been so low and what to do about it, I think, to be frank, your sponsoring the renewal of J51 will be a huge tool to do a better job in terms of getting units back online quickly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think the changes that have been authorized by the state, including the 100% reimbursement, the updated cost schedule, I think these will be like much, much, much more successful in terms of getting rent stabilized.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I will say, you know, under J51 historically, we saw far more co-ops taking advantage of that program than we did rent stabilized buildings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think part of our goals going forward will be to do really aggressive outreach to make sure that building owners, whether they have vacancies or deferred capital needs, are fully utilizing J51.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And we look forward to working with you to make sure that gets passed swiftly.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I think one thing that would be helpful, whether today or in public conversation around these numbers around vacancies, are the differences in methodology like you mentioned, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The housing vacancy survey takes a very...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's a very deep dive on exactly why each unit is vacant.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And there's a very, once you start drilling down, the vacant and available for rent is a much smaller number.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So it would be helpful, I don't know if you have this answer today, but if you can compare that 57,000 that HCR is reporting with the much smaller vacant and affordable, excuse me, vacant and available number that the HVS puts out.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As a first question and second question, is the methodology going to stay the same with the housing vacancy survey now that it's not going to be conducted by the Census Bureau?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And is there anything that we should anticipate or look for with the new release?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate the question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I do think we could dive deeper into your question about low-cost units within that universe of 57,000.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And I think I'll volunteer our head of our policy team who's here today to take note that we'll dig into that and get back to you on it.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: As it relates to the housing vacancy survey, again, we're

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: deep into it now and we are working with a new vendor, but I don't anticipate any changes to the housing vacancy survey that would make a comparison look back to the previous surveys challenging in any way.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And so, you know, I think we're just looking forward to getting to February when we'll release the draft report.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about HVS methodology changes now that Census Bureau isn't conducting it. Levy says no changes are anticipated that would complicate comparisons. Sanchez then asks for specific benchmarks distinguishing high-road from low-road landlords. Director Weaver describes metrics around qualified purchaser criteria, willingness to work with tenants, and smoothing the relationship between enforcement and preservation programs.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez round 2: Housing Vacancy Survey methodology and high road/low road landlord distinction

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, and then last question in this section.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Both the housing plan and the rental ripoff report borrow a term from the labor movement and rest a distinction between landlords who take the high road and those who take the low road.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you share what specific benchmarks you use to define each of these terms?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How should the city distinguish between owners that want to do the right thing and those that are intransigent?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What are the use cases for escalating enforcement actions supporting owners with financing and other tools?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And before you answer, I won't name the houser, but I had a conversation yesterday with a houser who is on the worst landlords list,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: has a lot of open B and C class violations, has a very, very high rate of rental arrears within the portfolio of properties,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: and really describes themselves and understands themselves as a good landlord, somebody who wants to do the right thing, but ends up on this list.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if you just look at the data, is one of the bad ones, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just very curious if you have...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: those specific benchmarks and how, if you could point us to the ways that rental ripoff report recommendations and the block by block plan contemplate working with the high road landlords.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, we've had a lot of discussion.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And we've had a lot of discussion at today's hearing about what constitutes a qualified purchaser and HPD's ongoing work to evaluate who they should be working within their preservation programs.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And so really we're talking about the same set of metrics and really making sure that the owners that we're working with have the capacity to manage extremely distressed buildings across their portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: At the same time, with this sort of high road distinction, we're also really looking to work with owners who want to work with their tenants.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And so we are really putting an emphasis on dialogue with residents and resident associations and a willingness to both work with us and also with people who live in their buildings themselves.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And so that communication and collaborative relationship is really important for our enforcement programs, but also our preservation programs.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Finally, to your question of a landlord who is wanting to do the right things, one of the things that we're hoping to be able to do

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: in partnership with the council in the coming years is to really smooth out that relationship between our enforcement programs and our preservation programs so that, for example,

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: we can discharge a building from the alternative enforcement program if it enters into a preservation deal with the city.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: And so I think there's a lot that we can do here.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: To really make sure that this distinction is meaningful and looking forward to continue to define it together.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: There have been many conversations that I've had with different landlord groups, you know, folks like Sponey, who are owners of small rent-stabilized properties, affordable housers who end up on lists like this.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And invariably, they have interesting ideas, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Like, you know, this idea that fines and fees do not inherently improve conditions for tenants.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So what if we could treat the good ones differently, I think is an interesting thing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, you convert your fines and fees to rent forgiveness, and then when rent...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Rent collections pick up again, those funds could go for improvement of the property.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I think that those kinds of ideas are interesting.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just putting in a plug for bringing them in and having more conversations.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Yeah, very much.

utterances.speaker: Director Weaver
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so I'm going to call on...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm going to recognize Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Call on Councilmember Ressler, followed by Councilmember Nurse for round two.

chapters.summary: Restler asks if HPD supports Intro 649 (LLC disclosure); Levy confirms general support with follow-up needed on enforcement and veil-piercing. Restler then raises poor conditions in new 421A construction in his district. Levy notes HPD has high design standards for financed projects, and Tagani says DOB continues updating building codes and construction sign-off processes.
chapters.title: CM Restler questions on LLC disclosure bill support and new construction quality

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I make an effort to say it at every hearing because it's so true.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are enormously fortunate to have you at the helm of this critically important committee.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Commissioner Levy, Director Weaver, it's good to see you both.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Commissioner Tagani.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Less so.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I will say, Commissioner Tagani, I have been really appreciative of how responsive your team has been when we've raised issues from the

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: jail in downtown Brooklyn where Deputy Commissioner Kelly has done a superb job, Commissioner Shahada in Brooklyn, Jason Rzezewski.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, across the board, your chief of staff, Sonia, have all been really responsive and helpful, and I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's the last nice thing I'm going to say to you for a while.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: A handful of things from me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll try to go fast.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I appreciate the testimony that said you support the goals of our LLC disclosure bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you support the bill?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we do generally support the bill.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we would like to have some follow-up conversations with you about what enforcement would look like.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: And then, right, also the challenge of making sure we are piercing the veil so that we are getting the right information posted.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But generally, yes, we support the bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Let's get it passed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Next up.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: All right, two more.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll do two or three more quick ones.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Our district, I think, was like the epicenter of 421A construction.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we are increasingly hearing from tenants that are experiencing brown water, elevators that don't work, just shitty conditions, excuse my French, in what is new construction.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: These are not buildings from 50 and 100 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is new construction.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As you're embarking on this bold and ambitious housing plan, do we need to rethink our standards of what we're requiring of developers to ensure that we're not continuing to get crappy conditions and new construction getting built across the city?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know if Commissioner Jagani wants to speak to it.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would say these buildings are no different than any other building in the city where we have high expectations for compliance and maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So if there are defects in construction, which should not have happened, but if there are defects in construction, we then should take action through our code enforcement offices to require corrections.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we don't want to be doing things.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, trying to fix these issues after a developer did a shoddy job is really not a great way to try to solve problems.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: We don't disagree.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So what can we do on the front end now as you're embarking on an ambitious new housing plan to try to set higher and better expectations so this doesn't continue to happen?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: The challenge here, I think, from my perspective, is that when HPD is financing a project, we have very high design guidelines and design guideline standards.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So we have a lot to say about what gets built and the quality of what gets built.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I would say in the private market, right, there are codes that I should maybe let Commissioner Dugani talk about that dictate what the standards are.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Frankly, we hear more often that the standards are onerous than we hear that they're too lax.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But if there are changes that you've had specifically that you think we should consider, we certainly would.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: I'll say quickly, I know we don't have a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: This is why we continue to update the building code.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: This is why the construction sign-off process before a temporary CO or CO is so critical.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: And, yes, we hear more often than not that people complain about the rigor than the laxness.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: But if there are specific issues that we have to dig into, we'd like to talk to you more about it.

utterances.speaker: Amin Tagani
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler raises 5,200 expiring EHV vouchers, noting 2,000 HPD households are being converted to HOME TBRA and 1,700 NYCHA households moved to HPD, but 3,400 remain with NYCHA only offered applications for Section 8/9 units. Levy says NYCHA has an 81% response rate. Restler expresses skepticism that families will actually be placed before December expiration.
chapters.title: CM Restler questions on expiring emergency housing vouchers and NYCHA response gap

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Chair, could I get one more question?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am deeply concerned about the expiring emergency housing vouchers, 5,200 of them.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I apologize if this has come up already today, but 5,200 vouchers expiring at the end of this year, thanks to the incompetence, ineptitude, and perhaps pure evil of the Trump administration.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My understanding is that 2,500 of these vouchers under HPD's purview have a path forward with the home tenant-based rental vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you confirm the accuracy there and that NYCHA has no solution for the similar 2,500 vouchers under their control?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Why not move all of those vouchers under HPD?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Can we do the home tenant-based rental vouchers for all 5,000-odd families that are otherwise in an incredibly difficult position and potentially

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Essentially at risk of homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What's the path here?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So I should correct the numbers and the record.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So the first 2,000 families that HPD had under our own EHV program are all being converted or offered conversion to TBRA, tenant-based rental assistance, which is paid for under home.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: There's an additional 1,700 families that were on NYCHA or individuals, households that were on NYCHA EHV

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: that we have moved over to HPD because we had additional home resources through Home ARP, which was a special allocation granted during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That is pretty much the capacity that we have for conversion from EHV to TBRA.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: That said, NYCHA is now...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How many are left over?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: So the 3,400 that remain within NYCHA's universe that are not being converted to TBRA are all being offered to fill out applications for NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Packed Section 8 units, regular Section 9 NYCHA units, and their own project-based vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I realize that NYCHA is not your responsibility, but that's not a particularly serious answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Yes, it is a serious answer, and they've had an 81% response rate from reaching out to that 3,400.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And you think that we're going to move people into Section 9 housing and into NYCHA apartments off those waiting lists in time before their vouchers expire in three months?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think that is the goal and that both agencies.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: Do you think anyone will move off of that?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I don't want to speak for NYCHA, but I think both agencies are working really diligently to make sure that we get the transition plans in place before the EHE subsidy expires.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I mean,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: In December.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You can model the waiting lists and look at the need.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think any families will move off of that waiting list into housing?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And you think a substantial number of them will?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I mean, I can't guess at what number will, but I think they've had a very high response rate, and I think those folks who really do need additional subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But a high response rate to completing an application is a different thing than actually accessing the housing support that they need.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Filling out an application is very nice.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's not all that helpful, right?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, people are being placed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, so do you have an expectation of the 3,400 delta of how many will get help?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I don't, but it's my understanding that NYCHA has been reporting regularly to the council on what the percentages are of both response and uptake, so I think we should...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're not particularly responsive to our request for information, but we'll look for more.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm going to call on Councilmember Brewer to read a statement on her legislation, followed by Councilmember Nurse for round two.

chapters.summary: Brewer presents her bill to authorize HPD and FDNY to inspect buildings for required street numbers during routine inspections, create a 311 complaint pathway for missing numbers, and take enforcement action. She traces the issue back to 1929 and her 2017 Local Law 26, noting that a decade later there is still no clear enforcement responsibility.
chapters.title: CM Brewer presents Intro 860 on building street number inspection and enforcement

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I want to acknowledge that we've been joined in person by Councilmember Zhuang and over Zoom by Councilmember Salam.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm across the street at another hearing that I'm co-chairing, so I'm sorry I wasn't here earlier, but I do want to talk about Intro 860, which is quite different than some of the others.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This has to do with addresses on buildings, and it's something that I have been talking about for a very long time, so I hope this bill passes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We all know that in many cases, it is important to have clearly

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: blade building numbers to help first responders, residents, delivery workers, tourists, and me trying to get to the next event.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And ensuring that every building is properly and visibly numbered strengthens public safety and makes navigating our neighborhoods easier, and it's also the law.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I will say that, you know, there have been many times, this New York Times story, even back to 1929, where people were so frustrated about this issue that there was no number on the building.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So fast forward to 2017, I was a Manhattan Borough President.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I passed Local Law 26 with Jumaane Williams, who was then in the council, to reinforce the display requirements and increase the civil penalty.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For failing to post street numbers, and the cost fine went from $25 to $250.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But crucial to this effort was the support of then Fire Commissioner Negro, who knew better than anyone

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that seconds count and response time is wasted when 911 callers, that's the hearing I am at across the street, cannot quickly identify the location of a life-threatening emergency.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A decade later, that's how many years it was,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We didn't know which agencies are responsible for enforcing this common sense law for both residential and commercial buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Believe me, we had no idea.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So building number violation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: remain severely underreported and as of today there's no way to officially report a missing building number to 311 or any other city agency.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So this intro 860, this is what it would do, would authorize HPD

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and the fire department to inspect buildings for required physical street numbers during their routine inspections of buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If either agency finds that the building is noncompliant, the agency may take enforcement actions consistent with the rules and regulations established by the Department of City Planning.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The bill would also create a new complaint pathway, 311, that would require either HPD or FDNY to proactively inspect the building regarding a missing or improperly displayed street number.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Owners would remain accountable for meeting basic legal and administrative requirements.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I certainly want to thank Tyler.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Isaiah Walls of the Council Legislative Division and Shula Puder for mine.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My support staff for making this happen.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know all these bills are important, but if you ask New Yorkers what is most important, it has two things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That goddamn ABC on the restaurant, which I don't care about, but they do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or I can't find the building.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I really hope that you support this bill, do you?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I'll start.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we do support the bill, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: I think we just want it to...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: work with you and with DCP, who's already writing rules based on the previous iteration of something comparable, just to make sure that we are not, we're all rowing in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Dina Levy
utterances.text: But generally, we 100% support the bill.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just in terms of housing, SRO housing, you need to purchase them on the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The Windermere on 57th Street and the Imperial Court on 79th Street.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I now want to turn it to Councilmember Nurse.
