utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: These measures are urgently needed to stabilize at-risk buildings, and we encourage the department to undertake proactive outreach to enroll as many buildings as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: We're also looking forward to working with the administration and the council to identify options for housing court diversion for 100% affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: And finally, while we are pleased that the Mamdani administration is experimenting with a public insurance option, we have concerns about timing, access, and scale, and which buildings will be prioritized, which are outlined in detail in our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: Moving on to code enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: Block by Block rightly emphasizes the critical importance of improving the city's system for enforcing the housing maintenance code.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: The focus on overhauling the system is welcome, and A&HD wholeheartedly...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: It supports the administration's approach of proactive enforcement targeting low-road landlords, expansion of various enforcement programs, and improved systems for engaging with tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: ANHD is also eager to work with the administration and the council to pursue deeper reforms not yet discussed in detail in the administration's plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: These include making it easier for tenants to withhold rent and receive abatements when faced with persistent violations, increasing penalty amounts, and establishing clear guardrails for any penalty adjustments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: Briefly on new construction, ANHD does commend the administration for an increased commitment to building deeply affordable housing in contrast to previous housing plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: However, as just referenced by my colleague here, the commitments in block by block still do not come close to meeting the scale of the need for affordable housing at the lowest income levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: Lastly, ANHD does urge the council to pass COPA, which is a valuable tool to empower tenants and help bring more housing into permanent affordability and responsible mission-driven ownership for long-term preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Peter Estes
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Daniel Manley, Robert Foster, Katie Mui, Maritza Rico.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And Kevin Kaprowski from Live on New York.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And whoever is ready can begin.

chapters.summary: Manley strongly supports Intro 1015 (J51 reauthorization), explaining it helps over 2,000 co-ops and condos with Local Law 97 carbon emissions limits afford energy efficiency upgrades, extends the program through 2036, and empowers HPD to update covered project lists biannually.
chapters.title: Danielle Manley (Urban Green Council) on J51 reauthorization and Local Law 97 compliance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: My name is Danielle Manley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: I'm the Associate Director for Policy at Urban Green Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: We're a nonprofit organization based here in New York City, and our mission is to decarbonize buildings for healthy and resilient communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: We strongly support Mayor Mamdani's commitment to making housing more affordable for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: The mayor's housing plan meets the moment with proposals that build more housing and lower the cost of owning and operating existing buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: In particular, Urban Green strongly supports the plan's proposed expansion of the J51 Reform Property Tax Abatement Program, J51R, and your proposal, Intro 1015, being considered today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: J51R is a key tool that helps eligible co-ops, condos, and multifamily buildings afford the capital improvements and maintenance repairs that they need to make.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: As you know, it's broadly available for a wide array of projects, and uniquely, J51R helps cover the cost of energy efficiency and electrification projects that support compliance with Local Law 97.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: We particularly support Intro 1015 because it helps owners navigate Local Law 97 in the following ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: First, it expands access to J51R.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Urban Green's data analysis shows that raising the assessed value threshold to $60,000 is going to allow more than 2,000 co-ops and condos that have carbon emissions limits use J51 to recoup costs for local 97 upgrades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: There's over 310,000 residential units in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: These are the buildings where everyday New Yorkers live, and those owners have been asking for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: This legislation offers them real help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: The changes now mean that half of all co-ops and condos with carbon emissions limits can use the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Second, this legislation extends the J51R program through 2036.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Many building owners and boards are making decisions today about projects to meet Local Law 97's 20 and 2035 limits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: This extension offers them the certainty to plan and finance those long-term capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Third, it increases the potential tax benefit that can make the difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: It increases the potential tax benefit that can make the difference in whether critical upgrades are financially feasible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: And last, it allows the program to evolve alongside Local Law 97 and emerging technologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: The legislation empowers HBD to consider cost-effective local 97 compliance upgrades, solutions when updating the list of covered projects, and it requires a review of that list at least every two years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: As you probably know, technologies to address energy efficiency and electrification are evolving every day, and this will ensure that New Yorkers can affordably access these emerging solutions over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: We look forward to working with HPD to ensure that that list reflects those new and lower cost upgrades as they become available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Finally, I'll close by saying the program is set to expire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: in June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: This update not only aligns affordability and decarbonization, it gives thousands of co-ops and condo owners the peace of mind that J51 will remain available for them in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: And so we thank you for your time today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Sanchez, this committee, and all council members in support of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rico urges expanding the NYC 1515 Rental Assistance RFP to include state-administered contracts, making the match pilot permanent, and closing the CHAP gap that excludes rent-stabilized buildings with regulatory agreements, which prevents domestic violence survivors in those buildings from accessing rental assistance.
chapters.title: Maritza Rico (New Destiny Housing) on supportive housing gaps and CHAP exclusions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez, Council Member Nurse, Council staff, and namely Ben.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: My name is Maritza.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: I am the Policy and Advocacy Manager at New Destiny Housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Chair, you know us, but for the record, we are the only organization in New York focused entirely on permanent housing for survivors of domestic violence, the leading cause of family homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And we also operate the first and largest federally funded rapid rehousing program for survivors in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We will submit a full written testimony, but I'll highlight the main points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: In regards to the housing plan, block by block, we want to talk about supportive housing, of course, particularly the supportive preservation program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: One fix that would let that commitment reach survivors now would be the accompanying NYC 1515 Rental Assistance RFP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Currently is open only to owners with city-administered service contracts, and that excludes every domestic violence supportive housing project because no city service funding existed for this population until NYC 1515 opened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: into survivors in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: So we urged HPD to expand eligibility in the next round to projects with state administered contracts and we asked that survivors be named a priority population as these resources are allocated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Regarding speed, we were thankful to be participants of the roundtables.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We're committing to helping

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: the administration implement those recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We have a platform called Fixing City FEPS on our website with our additional recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And namely, we want to name the Match Pilot Program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We would like for this...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: To be made permanent and extended beyond targeted developments and partner with population-specific providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you for CHAP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: It's great progress, and especially it's reached beyond the DHS shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Chair, may I wrap?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: But there's an important gap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: The eviction prevention category exclude rent-stabilized units, as you mentioned earlier, with regulatory agreements like us, New Destiny.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: So we continue to advocate for survivors living in community to be eligible regardless of the type of housing they're in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And then one more thing I want to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: I know this is not a general welfare or public housing hearing, but we have to ring the alarm on NYCHA EHVs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you so much, yourself and Lincoln Ressler, for doing that earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And finally, we hope that everyone's committed to passing COPA once and for all today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez, the committee, and the other council members out there.

chapters.summary: Moy warns of $200 million in potential HUD cuts through the Continuum of Care program, urges converting HASA units to NYC 1515, expediting sealed unit openings with NYPD, and expediting one-shot deal applications for supportive housing tenants to reduce court filings.
chapters.title: Katie Moy (Supportive Housing Network) on federal funding cuts and supportive housing vacancies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: My name is Katie Moy, and I am the Policy and Programs Manager at the Supportive Housing Network of New York, a membership organization representing over 200 nonprofits that develop, own, and operate supportive housing across the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: The network would first like to thank the City Council and the Progressive Caucus for your support over the last few years with the New York City 1515 Reallocation Plan, which has resulted in the promise of 5,000 new congregate units,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: a new supportive preservation program, and rental assistance for programs in need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: We also want to thank you for the inclusion of a flexible repair fund for supportive housing units in this year's budget advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: While the network remains neutral on the bills discussed today, we look forward to building on our collaboration with the Council as our members continue to face uncertainty at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: With looming unprecedented funding cuts from HUD, the city stands to lose close to $200 million through the Continuum of Care program, with no contingency plan in place to ensure tenants remain housed and programs stay open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: The network and its members urge the council and the administration to work with the state to identify feasible solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: to secure New York City's current supportive housing stock in the likely event that the federal administration is successful in reducing funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: In the meantime, the city can take steps right now to do the following, related to some of the topics discussed today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: One, address persistent vacancies in the HASA portfolio by supporting the conversion of HASA units to New York City 1515.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: Expanding access to those units to the people living on the street or in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: Two, working with the NYPD and the public administrator's offices to expedite the opening of sealed units, ensuring timely turnover and re-rentals to people experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: And lastly, third, advise the Department of Social Services to expedite the one-shot deal applications for tenants in supportive housing, reducing housing court filings, and supporting tenants in reducing arrears.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: The network is committed to continuing our work together to strengthen the supportive housing model and ensure that New Yorkers have access to safe and stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Moy
utterances.text: Thank you again.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks Manley for the full universe of units that could benefit from J51 expansion beyond the 310,000 with Local Law 97 limits. Manley agrees to research. Sanchez asks Rico about the administration's response on CHAP exclusions; Rico says they are unsatisfied and want buildings housing domestic violence survivors to be eligible.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez follow-up with Manley on J51 unit count and Rico on CHAP exclusions

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Two quick follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Danielle, you mentioned 300,000 to 350,000 units within co-ops and condos that could benefit from the J51 expansion.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate for the full universe of number of units that could benefit from this expansion?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Manley
utterances.text: Personally have the number outside of those with local law 97 carbon emissions limits, but I could look, I could probably get that for you, but I'm not, I'm not sure today.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Would help me with, you know, just making sure that my colleagues all sign on and we can get this passed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then my question for New Destiny is, what did you think of the administration's response on why regulatory agreement buildings were carved out of the CHAP program?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We're not satisfied with that response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We think that, for example, New Destiny houses many EHV recipients, for example, and we can't offer, or those tenants couldn't use CHAP, for example, to replace their EHV because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: all of our buildings, our 11 buildings, are excluded from that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We would love the opportunity to have this reconsidered so that, you know, our buildings that are housing domestic violence survivors can be eligible for CHAP.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your participation.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, the next panel is going to be Zach Steinberg, Edmundo Alex Gomez, and Mary Astrid Neusbaumer.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if you're here, Amalia de la Iglesia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Whoever is ready can begin.

chapters.summary: Steinberg acknowledges COPA improvements but says additional revisions are needed on lawsuit limits, timeline clarity, and administrative extensions. He strongly opposes Intro 649, arguing existing law already requires ownership disclosure and the bill raises privacy concerns by requiring public disclosure of beneficial owners including minors and passive investors.
chapters.title: Zach Steinberg (REBNY) expresses COPA concerns and opposes Intro 649

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: My name is Zach Steinberg, and I'm testifying on behalf of the Real Estate Board of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: I'd like to focus my remarks on Intro 905 and Intro 649.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: First, Intro 905, the Community Operative Purchase Act, or COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: REBNY appreciates our ongoing dialogue with the sponsor and appreciates the significant improvements that have been made to the legislation since last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: The current version applies to a narrow universe of properties, modifies the distress criteria, shortens the transaction timeline, and limits HPD's authority to extend deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: These are meaningful changes that make the bill more targeted and reduce the risk of disrupting transactions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: However, COPA remains a significant intervention into private property transactions, and additional revisions are needed to provide certainty for owners, lenders, and affordable housing investors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: We urge the Council to establish reasonable limits on lawsuits and penalties, clarify the timelines governing the right of first refusal process, and place firm limits on administrative extensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: We also urge the Council to ensure that future expansions of COPA scope occur through legislation rather than agency rulemaking, and to ensure that buildings that have remedied the conditions that triggered COPA coverage have a clear path to exit the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: These changes would help ensure the bill is predictable, administerable, and does not unintentionally discourage investment in housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: Second, Rebney has serious concerns with the 649.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: Existing law already requires building owners to disclose ownership and management information in building lobbies, ensuring that tenants know who owns and manages the building and who to contact when issues arise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: Intro 649 goes much further by requiring the public disclosure of beneficial owners and other individuals behind ownership entities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: This raises significant privacy concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: and could expose owners and their families to harassment or other unwanted contact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: In some cases, the bill could require disclosure of individuals with no operational role in the property, including minors or passive investors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: The city already has mechanisms to obtain ownership information for legitimate government and law enforcement purposes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: We do not believe the additional public disclosure required by this bill is justified by any corresponding public benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zach Steinberg
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and consideration, and we look forward to working with the council and administration to advance policies that increase housing production, preserve existing housing, and improve outcomes for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Nussbaumer recommends funding one year of stability services for vouchered households to prevent evictions, contracting housing navigators to help voucher holders secure units, and three additional recommendations including allowing nonprofit staff to sign off on City FEPS inspections.
chapters.title: Mary Astrid Nussbaumer (Anthos Home) on eviction prevention and housing navigators

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Clara Sanchez, Deputy Speaker Williams, and members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: I'm Mary Astrid Nussbaumer, an aftercare specialist at Anthos Home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: We help New Yorkers move from shelter into homes faster and are in the Family Homelessness Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: We are grateful that the mayor's office and the council recognize the severity of the homelessness crisis and are energized by block by block.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Based on our experience, here are some implementation recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: For 1.2, reduce eviction cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Fund at least one year of stability services for moved-in vouchered households.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Helping people recertify vouchers or fix missing payments keeps small problems from snowballing into eviction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: In fiscal year 24, the city spent $484 million on one-shot deals, about $10K per household, twice the median arrears for affordable housing tenants for nonpayment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Prevention costs far less.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: For 6.2, strengthen housing search and lease-up support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Contract with housing navigators to help voucher holders secure units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: For a voucher holder facing discrimination and competition, finding a home is hugely difficult and it is harder still for those with complex needs like high health need households.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Designated navigators expand the supply of units, ease shelter staff workloads, and move in more people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Our written testimony includes three more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Resolve minor inspection fixes without re-inspection, allow nonprofit staff to sign off on all city FEPS inspections, and expand the match pilot so nonprofits can also refer people to set aside units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Thank you again.

chapters.summary: Gomez cites 96,000 people in shelters nightly, 73% of extremely low-income households severely rent-burdened, and only 21% of new affordable units available to extremely low-income households over the last decade. He calls for 12,000 units per year for five years reserved for homeless and extremely low-income New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Alex Gomez (Coalition for the Homeless) calls for 60,000 units for homeless New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: My name is Alex Gomez with Coalition for the Homeless and Homes for NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Homes for NYC is a coalition of service providers, advocacy organizations, and experts working to increase affordable housing for homeless and extremely low-income New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: We are calling on the mayor to increase capital funding and build 60,000 units of affordable housing for homeless and extremely low-income New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Along with some of my other colleagues here as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Last month, over 96,000 people, 96,000 people,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Slept in New York City shelters on average every night, including over 30,000 children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: That does not include people sleeping unsheltered or the estimated 200,000 New Yorkers doubled and tripled up in someone else's home before they inevitably end up in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: The number of people without homes in the cities continue to increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Homelessness is the consequence of our housing crisis, specifically the lack of homes renting for prices that low-income households can afford.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: 73% of extremely low-income households in New York are severely rent-burdened, as previously mentioned, meaning they pay more than 50% of their monthly income on rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Evictions disproportionately impact extremely low-income homes as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Between 2020 and 2025, the top 10 zip codes with the highest eviction rates were concentrated in the Bronx, where more than half of households earned less than $53,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: That's right at the very low income level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Yet despite record levels of affordable housing production in recent years, only 21% of new affordable housing units over the last decade

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: were available to extremely low-income households, 21% for a vast majority of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: While block by block contains some significant commitments to address homelessness, it fails to articulate a vision of housing production that would significantly reduce the number of people experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: May I wrap?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: The production target falls short for the lowest income New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: A 40% increase in homeless set-aside units does not come close to the 50,000 households currently in shelter,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: nor do the 24,000 units of affordable housing for ELI households in 2027 and 2028 are going to be able to match that 50,000 households in shelter as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: So we're calling on the city to commit to 12,000 units of truly affordable housing a year for the next five years, 60,000 units in total reserved for homeless and extremely low-income New Yorkers, because it is time for the city to build housing for those who need it most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Next panel is Ravnak Zamal, Jessica Balgobin, Amalia de la Iglesia, and Tussif Hassan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, she's Iglesias, right, Amelia?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And the following panel will be from Local 3 so that you are ready.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: So whoever is ready can begin.

chapters.summary: De la Iglesia describes absentee landlords extracting profit from East New York buildings while tenants live with unsafe conditions, and urges passage of COPA to give community land trusts the opportunity to purchase at-risk buildings and keep housing affordable.
chapters.title: Amalia de la Iglesia (East New York CLT) on COPA as tool against speculation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: Hi, thank you, Chair Sanchez and members of the committee for holding today's hearing and for the opportunity to testify in favor of Intro 905 COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: My name is Amalia de la Iglesia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: I'm the housing campaign organizer for the East New York Community Land Trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: As a tenant organizer living and working in East Brooklyn, I see the impact of speculation and landlord negligence every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: A large part of the housing stock in East New York is owned by absentee landlords who do not live in the neighborhood and who are extracting maximum profit from their buildings at tenants'expense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: Low-income tenants and their families are paying half of their income in rent while living with unsafe conditions, including lack of heat and hot water, mold, collapsing ceilings, and pest infestations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: At best, tenants are caught in a cycle of fighting tooth and nail for basic repairs with no end in sight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: At worst, they're displaced as their homes are deregulated and flipped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: COPA is a critical tool to disrupt this cycle, protect the buildings that need it most, and allow people to stay in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: When buildings in disrepair or with expiring affordability restrictions are put up for sale, it's the city's responsibility to make sure that housing remains affordable and is put

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: in responsible hands, like community land trusts, rather than sold off to another absent landlord.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amalia de la Iglesia
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Balgobin describes threats to Indo-Caribbean communities in Queens from speculative corporations and predatory landlords, reports engaging 2,500 community members and collecting 300 postcards supporting COPA, and urges the Council to pass it.
chapters.title: Jessica Balgobin (Queens CLT/Chaya CDC) on COPA and community momentum

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: Dear Councilmember Sanchez and members of the Housing and Buildings Committee, thank you for holding today's hearing and for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: My name is Jessica Balgabin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: I am a lifelong resident of Queens and a CLT organizer with Queens Community Land Trust at Chaya CDC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: When my family immigrated from Guyana to South Queens 30 years ago, they established roots in neighborhoods like Richmond Hill and South Ozone Park that reflected the needs of our communities as Indo-Caribbeans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: However, over the last few years, previously bustling Caribbean commercial corridors like Jamaica Avenue lost mom-and-pop shops to big corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: The cultural integrity of these communities are now threatened by speculative corporations and predatory landlords, and the lack of deeply affordable housing across neighborhoods like Queens Village, Jamaica, and South Ozone Park is of utmost concern to residents and CLT members alike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: Tenants like myself can no longer afford to pay their rents and stay in the neighborhoods we are deeply rooted in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: We urgently need Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, or COPA, into 905 that will give vetted nonprofits, including community land trusts, the first chance to purchase certain at-risk multifamily buildings when a landlord decides to sell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: COPA will allow for communities like those we work with and live in to stabilize and expand the supply of permanently affordable homes that New Yorkers are in desperate need of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: There is real community momentum in favor of COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: My team and I engaged over 2,500 community members and colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: collected more than 300 postcards signed in support of COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: We can take measurable steps to help prevent ongoing gentrification and displacement from wreaking havoc across Queens and beyond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: I urge you to pass COPA now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Balgobin
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Amal describes a tenant named Enrique trapped in his building by a broken elevator, tenants who organized, called the city, went to court, and withheld rent but still face neglect. He argues COPA would give tenants a real chance to shape what happens when buildings are sold.
chapters.title: Rinox Amal (Chaya CDC) on tenant conditions and COPA

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez and this committee for allowing me to testify in support of COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: My name is Rinox Amal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: I'm a lifelong Jackson Heights resident and a communications and neighborhood development associate at Chaya CDC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: I work with Queens residents fighting for stable, affordable, community-controlled housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: At Chaya, our organizers have been organizing tenants in Jamaica.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: For years, families in multiple buildings have lived with mold, rodents, leaks, unreliable heat and hot water, and elevators that repeatedly break down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: One resident, Enrique, has had to cancel appointments and miss time with his family because he cannot safely climb the stairs when the elevator fails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Imagine being trapped inside your own home, not just because of your health, because the person responsible for your building refuses to keep it safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: These tenants have done everything they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: They organized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: They called the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: They went to court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: They withheld rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Withheld rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Still, the neglect continues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Then there are situations where a building goes under foreclosure, potentially changing ownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: After years of fighting simply to live with dignity, these families could still be shut out of the decision about who owns their homes next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: As an organization, we, along with our partners and the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Tenants have ensured that three buildings that were going under foreclosure will not continue to be owned by the same predatory landlord.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: But we have no guarantee that the next landlord will be any better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: When we talk about housing, we are not just talking about properties and transactions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: We are talking about whether an older resident can make it to an appointment, whether a parent can put their child to bed without worrying about mold, whether a family can feel secure or must constantly wonder if the next landlord will force them out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: This is why COPA matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: It would give qualified, mission-driven nonprofits an opportunity to purchase covered buildings before they were sold in the open market.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Tenants could partner with a community land trust to make repairs, preserve affordability, and create housing that is accountable to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Home should mean safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: It should mean stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: It should mean knowing that your family will still have a place in the community you help build.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Too often, tenants are the last to know and the first to suffer when their buildings are sold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: COPA gives them a real chance to shape what happens next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: No one should have to fight this hard just to feel at home safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: I urge the council to pass COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rinox Amal
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hassan describes how corporations buy rent-stabilized buildings as assets rather than homes, using deterioration as a strategy to push out low-income tenants of color. He argues COPA would disrupt this speculation cycle and allow community ownership.
chapters.title: Tausif Hassan (Chaya CDC) on speculation as business model and COPA

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Sanchez, committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: My name is Tausif Hassan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: I'm the Associate Director of Housing Stability at Chaya CDC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: You've heard about our organization from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: I work with the tenant organizing team where we organize tenants in rent-stabilized buildings all over Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Buildings owned by some of the worst landlords in the city, like Zara, Bronstein, Summit, and Pinnacle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: And we're also in the process of organizing a community land trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: You've heard about the conditions that tenants face from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Most of the tenants that we work with are working class, people of color, immigrants, and they face horrible conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Meanwhile, their landlords are consistently on the worst landlords list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: They're billionaires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: They're corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: They're creating and maintaining systemic conditions of neglect and harassment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: And that's because their business model is to push out low-income tenants for whiter and wealthier tenants that can afford higher rents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: These landlords aren't in the business of providing dignified housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: They're in the business of extracting maximum profits from what they see as assets in the shape of buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: And some of them have amassed portfolios of dozens of buildings over the years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Corporations have been buying up multifamily homes from individual owners at an accelerated rate since the 2000s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: And now they make up the vast majority of rent-stabilized landlords.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Now most of them are...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: The sales of rent-stabilized buildings simply transfer ownership from one corporation to another.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Even distressed properties are mostly transferred to manage financial liabilities and create portfolios, not to actually address conditions for tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: This illustrates what the buildings really represent to landlords and that it's stocks, not homes for New Yorkers to live and build community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Conditions have deteriorated and rents have skyrocketed because of this frenzy of speculation that has gone on uninterrupted for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: New Yorkers deserve to live in dignified, affordable homes, and that's why we need COPA to allow tenants to have a fighting chance to disrupt speculation and bring housing under community control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tausif Hassan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Kudos on, what was it, 2,500 conversations?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This is the third time that we've heard this, that I literally, I have heard this piece of legislation, and I just thank you for all that you've done to get us here and

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: urge you to stay at the table, keep calling my colleagues who may be on the fence about the bill just so that we can get the traction we need to finally pass COPA.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I will now call the next panel from Local 3.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And Local 3, kudos to you for sending me the testimony in advance.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Michael Jordan, Michael Grunert, Michael Payumbe, I'm sorry for the pronunciation, and then from Local 1, Freddie Delegati.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are you making trouble over there?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Ardian?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We also have Richard Gilligan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Richard?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So Freddie is not testifying?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And whoever is ready can begin.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can we restart?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I want you to get cut off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: Again.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, there we go.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Jordan urges requiring project labor agreements for affordable housing construction and warns that 485X creates incentives to stay at 99 units to avoid stronger labor requirements. He argues public subsidy should require family-sustaining jobs, not poverty wages.
chapters.title: Mike Jordan (Local 3 IBEW) on project labor agreements and 485X concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: So thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: I am Mike Jordan, a business representative for Local 3, International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: I'm here in support of project labor agreements for affordable housing construction and also to urge the city to make sure that 485X does not become a race to the bottom on construction wages and working conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: New York City needs housing, there's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: But the answer cannot be to subsidize housing while subsidizing poverty for the workers who build it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: When taxpayers provide billions of dollars in tax benefits and other public support,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: housing construction, we have a responsibility to demand something in return.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: Affordable homes, good quality construction, and family-sustaining jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: This is exactly why PLAs matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: A project labor agreement establishes labor standards before construction begins, provides a trained workforce, consistent work rules, safety protections, benefits, and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: It ensures the public investment creates a pathway into the middle class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: We should also be honest about the incentives created by 485X.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: When the rules become significantly different at the 100-unit threshold, developers have an incentive to stay at 99 units rather than build more housing and accept stronger labor and affordability requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: This is not a housing policy we should encourage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: We should not be creating incentives to build fewer apartments or to reduce labor standards simply to qualify a tax benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: If a developer is receiving public subsidy, the public should receive a public benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: This means more affordable apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: It means construction workers earning wages that allow them to support their family, community hiring,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: pathways into apprenticeships and into the middle class, opportunities for New Yorkers who want to enter the trades, and then, of course, safe, quality construction that will serve our communities for generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: We cannot pit affordable housing against good jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: The workers building affordable housing deserve to be able to afford housing themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Grunner briefly connects CM Restler's earlier complaint about subpar new construction to the need for union labor, stating 'if you want better buildings, build union.'
chapters.title: Michael Grunner (Local 3) on union construction quality

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Perfect timing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Gomez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: My name is Michael Grunner, and I'm a proud member of the IBW Local Union No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: I'm not going to bore you and repeat all the same things that he just said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: I'm going to bring up that a council member earlier mentioned subpar new construction residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: And all I can say to that is if you want better buildings, you want better home lives, if you want better communities, you want to build a better New York, build a union.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gilligan urges strict adherence to building codes, opposes plastic piping (PEX) due to Legionella and microplastic contamination risks, warns against creating a 'cheaper, dangerous code for affordable housing,' opposes unchecked modular/prefabrication as transferring work away from New Yorkers, and urges PLAs on subsidized construction.
chapters.title: Richard Gilligan (Plumbers Local 1) on building codes, plastic piping, and modular concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Well, at this point, I'm going to say good afternoon, Chair Sanchez and members of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: My name is Richard Gilligan, business agent at large at UA Plumbers Local Union No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: I'm testifying on behalf of Paul O'Connor, Local One's business manager.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: On behalf of the approximately 6,000 skilled plumbers, gas fitters, and apprentices represented by Local One, thank you for the opportunity to testify regarding Mayor Mondami's Block by Block, the housing plan for New Era.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Local One is proud of the role our union and its members have played for more than 30 years in developing and strengthening New York City's building and plumbing codes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: The mayor's housing plan should strictly adhere to those codes and the high standards they established for safety and quality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: The commitment should include prohibiting plastic piping and other inferior materials where safer, more durable alternatives are available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Local One is particularly concerned about PEX and similar plastic piping because research has demonstrated

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: that piping material can affect biofilm formation and conditions associated with the growth and presence of Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Plastic piping is also widely recognized as the leading contributor of microplastic contamination in drinking water and commonly leach the chemicals used in their manufacture as water passes through them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: We should be strengthening plumbing standards, not compromising them to reduce construction costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Doing so would create two distinct sets of plumbing codes, a cheaper, dangerous code for affordable housing and vulnerable population it would serve, and a code for those that can afford safer materials installed by qualified and experienced union workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Local One will always support building more housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Our members understand the depth of New York City's housing shortage because they live here, they raise families here, and they work every day to keep the city functioning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: A serious housing plan must create enough affordable and workforce housing to give our apprentices and other working people a genuine opportunity to put down roots and remain in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Supporting more housing cannot mean abandoning the safeguards that protect workers, residents, and the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: As block-by-block plan removed from a proposal to implementation,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Projects eligible for the 485 tax incentive must fully comply with all applicable wage and labor requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: The city must also prevent developers from structuring projects, including 99-unit buildings, to evade those obligations and must ensure that the labor protections exist on every covered job site, not merely on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Local 1 Strolling encourages the Mamdami administration to use project labor agreements as broadly and as practical on all affordable housing construction receiving substantial city assistance, along with the meaningful protection against wage and theft worker

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: exploitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Safety must remain equally central.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Building more housing does not require weakening the standards that protect construction workers, future residents, and the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: If New York intends to increase the pace and scale of construction, strong safety standards, skilled tradespeople, and effective inspection become more essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Local One is particularly concerned about proposals that rely heavily on modular construction to the extent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: that they may involve off-site prefabrication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: For organized labor, the unchecked expansion of off-site prefabrication presents an

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: existential threat because it can transfer substantial portions of the construction work away from New York City job sites and away from New Yorkers who would otherwise perform this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: It also could potentially bypass prevailing wage requirements, project labor agreements, registered apprenticeship programs, local hiring opportunities, contractor accountability, and righteous protections embodied by the New York City Construction Code.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: For these reasons, Local 1...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Respectfully request that modular construction and prefabrication be removed from the plan rather than established as a potential model for the city's supporting housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: The city's commitment to housing must also include homes in New Yorkers already occupied.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Please conclude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Especially those operated by New York City Housing Authority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Repairing and modernizing NYCHA must remain a central priority in any comprehensive housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Palumbo describes the incentive to build 99-unit buildings to avoid construction wage requirements under 485X, arguing this hurts the middle class and that the housing crisis should not be solved by pitting workers against housing.
chapters.title: Michael Palumbo (Local 3) on 485X 99-unit loophole

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: Chair Sanchez, Michael Palumbo from Local 3, Residential Division.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: I'm here today, I believe, in the goal of 485X.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: New York City needs more housing, and we need more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: But I believe there's a problem with the way the program is structured.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: Under the 485X, there's a major difference between a project with 99 homes and a project with 100 units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: Projects with 100 or more units are subject to construction wage requirements, while 6 to 99 unit category are different requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: This creates a very strong incentive to stop at 99, and that's what I believe we need to fix.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: We need to build more housing, but we need to make sure that incentives actually encourage developers to build more rather than encourage them to stop just below the threshold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: As an electrician, I see firsthand what goes into construction of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: The men and women who build New York housing deserve to earn a wage that allows them to support their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: We should be creating opportunities for people to enter the skilled trades, build careers, and become part of the middle class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: So my request is simple, to stop the 99-unit loophole, which lowers labor costs and overall hurts the middle class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: At the end of the day, New York's housing crisis shouldn't be solved by putting workers and housing against each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: We should be able to have more housing, more affordability, and more middle-class construction jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: And that's what I believe 45X should and can accomplish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Palumbo
utterances.text: Thank you for your time today.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for specific recommendations on the 99-unit loophole. Grunner suggests preventing subdivision of parcels to create multiple 99-unit buildings and requiring developers to build what the property can hold. Jordan notes shared foundations and driveways as red flags. Gilligan requests seats on advisory committees. Sanchez asks for written follow-up on shared infrastructure issues.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez follow-up with labor panel on 485X loophole and legislative solutions

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: A follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So first of all, there's the legislative task force and the mayor's construction safety working group.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I guess I forget what they're calling it, but just making sure that Local 3, Local 1 are on those is very important to make sure you're in the room to lift up these recommendations around plastic piping and modular.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: On the 485X problem, do you have a recommendation on legislative change, or is it a Department of Buildings practice?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is it about the way that site plans are reviewed?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have specific recommendations about what we should be doing and looking into?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, if it's obvious that a property can easily hold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: More than 99 units, you know, even 150 units, you shouldn't be allowing them to stop at 99.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: Like, they should be making more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: We need more housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: Now, that number changes significantly in the amount of affordable housing units from 99 to 150 also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: You're looking at 20%, you know, of 99 to 25 or more percent of 150, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: It adds up to be a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: And then subdivision of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: of the parcels of lands to then build 99, you know, unit loophole buildings, I would group them all back as one and, you know, make them be a 150 plus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: If I could just expand on it for one second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: So I just think there's situations potentially where you may have a piece of property or parcel where they're breaking it up into three addresses, but yet sharing a foundation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: It's one foundation for three separate addresses, and they're sharing driveways and common walkways and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mike Jordan
utterances.text: So I think that's another potential problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: And if I may, as far as the committees and the advisory committees are concerned, Local One asks for a seat at the table on some of those committees and give us the opportunity to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: inject our expertise into the subjects that are being discussed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Gilligan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I will just ask for a follow-up, especially on those issues.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: There's a common driveway.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: There's shared infrastructure, things that you're seeing on the ground in addition to just hovering at the 99 units.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That would be very helpful because then we can follow up with buildings and see if we can put a stop to it with these definitions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Grunner
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Next panel.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Logan Fares, Nadia Swanson, Martha Sickles, and Faiza Azam.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You just need to fill out a slip.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Open New York.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, whoever's ready can begin.

chapters.summary: Azam strongly supports Intro 1015 (J51 reauthorization), noting it would benefit 350,000 homeowners and help them comply with Local Law 97 clean energy transitions. She urges the Council to pass it immediately.
chapters.title: Faiza Azam (ALIGN/Climate Works for All) on J51 and Local Law 97

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Apologies for my snacking.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Hello, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Hi, y'all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: My name is Faiza Azam, and I am the climate and labor organizer for ALIGN, the Alliance for a Greater New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: I also coordinate the Climate Works for All Coalition, which is made of 26 labor unions, climate and environmental justice organizations, and community groups dedicated to tackling the climate crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: In 2019, we were an instrumental part in passing and advocating for Local Law 97.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: As you all know, 70% of the total emissions in New York City comes from our buildings, and that is why Climate Works for All has been strongly advocating to limit those emissions, but with that comes some

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: hurdles for some homeowners, and that is why Climate Works for All is here to strongly advocate for the passage of Intro 1015 that reauthorizes J51 tax abatement for co-op and condo owners and homeowners in general.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: This would not only benefit 350,000 homeowners across the city, but also benefit many in low-income communities, as we've heard earlier in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Climate Works for All has been strongly advocating with state legislators and state elected officials to pass J51 in the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: budget this past session for FY27, and we will continue to advocate for it since the bill is now aimed at focusing toward localized municipalities to pass J51.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Homeowners have been struggling when it comes to complying with clean energy transitions for their energy bills getting skyrocketing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Skyrocketing and affordability is extremely important, and for that to successfully enforce and implement Local 97, we need to ensure that New York is supporting our...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Your constituents with the proper financial means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Implementing Local 97 means that there is a piece of the puzzle where you are helping with that budgetary aspect, and we strongly urge that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Faiza Azam
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sickles supports J51 reauthorization, comparing today's modernization crisis to the one that led to J51's original 1955 enactment. She notes rising construction and operating costs, and that as federal and state climate support retreats, J51 becomes even more critical.
