chapters.title: Martha Sickles on J51 as critical tool for building modernization

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Hey, Martha.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: My name is Martha Sickles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: I'm principal of Urbicon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: I'm also a member of the Climate Works for All Coalition and the Green Co-op Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to attend and express support for the mayor's housing plan and the seven legislative items that are being discussed at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: I'm going to be submitting written testimony, but I'd like to make just a few points about support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: Of intro 1015, which

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: which is the revision and authorization of J-51.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: As colleagues have discussed, this bill was passed by the state legislature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: It is critical to providing a funding resource for homeowners, co-ops, condos, and owners of rental buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: The revision and reauthorization of this bill will help to provide and create

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: healthier, cleaner, more efficient, more affordable homes for low- and moderate-income renters, cooperative shareholders, and condominium residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: It was first enacted in 1955 to address a health, a public health, and building modernization crisis in substandard housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: And we are facing a similar situation today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: The similar modernization crisis is building owners face increasing regulations, requirements, and new laws designed to improve public safety, reduce carbon emissions, and provide prevailing wages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: These are all valuable public goods that warrant public support to help building owners implement them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: There was a recent study done, released by the New York Housing Conference, conducted by Hunter students that indicate the sources of rising costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: for both operation and construction of buildings, and J51 will assist in addressing some of these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: And as we face federal and state retreat from support of climate policy and funding, J51 will be useful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha Sickles
utterances.text: I also hope that we can act quickly to educate the public and that this program can get up and running soon.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time.

chapters.summary: Swanson describes 6,000 homeless youth with only 1,000 shelter beds, asks DOB to create exceptions for overnight sleeping in drop-in centers, and requests a priority review process for nonprofit housing providers. She reports 20 newly developed beds sitting empty for months while 450 youth wait, due to DOB approval delays.
chapters.title: Nadia Swanson (Ali Forney Center) on youth homelessness and DOB approval delays

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Thank you, Martha.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: My name is Nadia Swanson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Director of Advocacy and Global Programs at the Ali Fornay Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: And I first want to give my profound thanks to you, to Speaker Menon, and all the members that supported CHAP, as you've been doing, and giving youth access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: I can say whenever I get to tell our case managers, like, good news that's going to come their way, I usually get a lot of excitement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Every person I told just sighed with relief that this was happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: It's going to make a huge difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: We support the bills discussed today, but I want to focus on two issues that DOB can change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Today, more than 6,000 youth and young adults experience homelessness in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: There are more than 1,000 beds available to serve them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Since 2015, our drop-in center has operated 24-7 as a band-aid for a larger problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: There are simply not enough shelter beds for homeless young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Before then, youth slept in our center during the day because they had spent the night awake on the streets trying to stay safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Letting them sleep overnight gave them their days back and the ability to take the steps towards stable housing and independence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: The model worked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: It ultimately led to five 24-7 youth drop-in centers across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Then in 2023, on one of the coldest days of the year, the city ordered providers to remove sleeping accommodations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Years later, we still have no reasonable explanation as to why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Meanwhile, young people sit and drop in center chairs overnight, sometimes for up to six months, waiting for a shelter bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: We're asking DOB to create an exception with Group B and A3 classifications that would allow temporary non-residential overnight sleeping on cots with low barrier safety standards designed specifically for drop-in centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: The second issue is the speed of DOB approvals for organizations creating desperately needed housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: We're asking DOB to establish a priority review process for nonprofit community service organizations, particularly those creating shelter and housing for vulnerable New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: In October 2025, we cut the ribbon on 20 newly developed beds that remain empty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Well, approximately 450 young people are on a wait list, and we could have served 70 youth in the past year at that site.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: We spent significant resources developing the property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: We spent money to expedite, and it should not have taken this long to get a walkthrough to be able to implement these changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: So I think you understand why this is so necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Connors supports Intro 657 (Safer Homes Act), Intro 178 (Office of Conversion Assistance), and the housing plan's inclusion of shared housing and citywide TOD. He urges the Council to ensure more housing is built near transit and that wealthy neighborhoods stop being 'frozen in amber' at the expense of communities of color.
chapters.title: Jack Connors (Open New York) on conversions, housing plan, and transit-oriented development

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: I'm Jack Connors, City Legislative Manager at Open New York, a statewide grassroots advocacy group that pushes for more homes and lower rents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Thank you to Chair Sanchez and members of the committee for the opportunity to speak in support of Intro 657, Intro 178, and Mayor Mamdani's housing plan this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: For too long, housing scarcity has allowed negligent landlords to subject upwards of 350,000 New Yorkers to unsafe and unconscionable conditions for years, if not decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Insurance 657, the Safer Homes Act, empowers HPD to advocate on these tenants'behalf by reopening the third-party transfer program with expanded tenants'rights to form HDFC co-ops and critical guardrails like eliminating the block pickup provision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Open New York is also proud to support Councilmember Epstein's Intro 178, which would create an Office of Conversion Assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: So far this year, the city has permitted 74 office conversions that will yield more than 10,000 new homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Such conversions are a critical tool in building the 700,000 homes we'll need in the next decade to meet current and future demand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Still, complicated permitting and building code requirements remain persistent barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: An Office of Conversion Assistance can help applicants navigate these processes and identify reforms to streamline future applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Turning to Mayor Mamdani's housing plan, we're pleased to see the Safer Homes Act and Intro 66 Councilmember Maloney's shared housing bill, as well as citywide TOD included in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: It is priorities of this administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: We hope to see the council build up the city for all and fair housing framework to ensure that a little more housing is built in every neighborhood, especially near subway, rapid bus, and commuter rail service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: For too long, wealthy neighborhoods have remained frozen in amber at the expense of communities of color, which face extreme displacement pressure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: We urge the council to embrace the citywide nature of our housing crisis and partner with the admin to co-locate public goods with housing, comprehensively reform our building code, and allow more New Yorkers to live near the transit that they depend on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: An unnamed Mason Tenders speaker describes how labor brokers charge clients $30-50 per hour per worker while paying workers near minimum wage, relying on mass incarceration and poverty to suppress wages, and urges the city to take a 'no labor broker pledge' and expand the $40 CJA wage standard.
chapters.title: Mason Tenders speaker on labor broker exploitation in construction

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So whoever's ready can start.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Hello, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Construction has historically provided a pathway into the middle class for New Yorkers without a four-year college degree.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Equality construction career can allow someone to support a family, access health care, safer retirement, and build long-term financial security.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But that opportunity is lost when developers use low-wage labor brokers to recruit vulnerable workers and pay them near minimum wage without meaningful benefits, job security, or a pathway to advancement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The business model of a labor broker is based on charging the third-party clients an hourly markup on the rate of pay for each worker provided.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The workers are paid substandard wages, while the labor broker contractor gets paid $30 to $50 per hour for each worker.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They rely on the system of mass incarceration and poverty to suppress wages and create a pipeline of temporary laborers who do the most dangerous work on construction sites.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Workers build affordable housing while struggling to afford housing themselves.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Public investment generates development, but not the economic mobility.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Our communities were promised.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This is a policy choice, and the city can make a difference.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As the city implements block by block, workers must be at the forefront.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We are asking the city to take a no labor broker pledge, expand the $40 standard of CJA that passed this past December, and ensure that developers receiving public support provide safe conditions, meaningful benefits,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: transparent employment practices, and real pathways into construction careers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: George describes inconsistent NYCHA processes where some developments vote on PACT/Trust/Section 9 options while others are selected for PACT without resident votes, creating confusion and distrust. He urges requiring transparent resident elections before any major conversion model proceeds.
chapters.title: Infinite George on NYCHA transparency and resident voting rights

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Should I go or are we going to reset?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: My name is Infinite George, and I work directly with NYCHA residents across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: I'm here because residents are deeply concerned about the lack of transparency surrounding decisions that will determine the future of their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: NITRE residents know that their development needs major repairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: They live every day with broken elevators, leaks, mold, heating problems, and years of deferred maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Residents want investment and improvement, but they also want and deserve a meaningful role in deciding how those improvements happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Right now, the process is inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: In some developments, residents participate in an election to choose among the Public Housing Preservation Trust, PAC, or remaining in traditional Section 9 program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: At other developments, residents learn that their homes have already been selected for RADA PAC without having the opportunity to vote on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: This inconsistency creates confusion and distrust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Residents do not understand why one development received a vote while another does not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: They are often unsure how the development was selected, what decisions have already been made, and how a conversation will affect

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: property management, repairs, resident rights, employment opportunities, and daily life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Information sessions and resident engagement meetings are important, but they are not the same as giving residents the power to decide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Nature residents are the people who live with the consequences of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: They should receive clear, accessible information about every option, including the benefits, risks, financing structure, management changes, construction plans, and resident protections before any decision is made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: We are asking the city to require a transparent resident election process before any nature development proceeds with PAC-RAD, the Preservation Trust, or another major conversion model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Every eligible resident should have the opportunity to vote, and every development should be governed by the same and clear, consistent rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: In closing, public housing belongs to the public, and residents must be at the center of decisions about its future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: No major change should happen to a nature development without informed consent of the people who call it home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Infinite George
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Favor describes how the Construction Justice Act is already working with responsible developers paying $40/hour, but some developers use labor brokers paying poverty wages on subsidized projects. He specifically names Marin Workforce/Apex Labor Solution working on Hudson Companies projects, noting some workers live in shelter while building affordable housing.
chapters.title: Justice Favor (Local 79) on Construction Justice Act and labor broker exploitation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: My name is Justice Faven.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: I'm a field representative of the Mason Tenders District Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: I started as a construction laborer, and I was born and raised in public housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: I'm proof that a fair wage and a benefit package and construction can transform your life and the lives of others around you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Like it did for me and my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: I'm here to make sure our city has construction justice so that our communities have access to family-sustaining wages and affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: New York City residential construction industry can provide good wages and benefits while continuing to build the housing our city urgently needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: We are proud and excited that the Construction Justice Act passed by the City Council and is a key part of the Mayor's Housing Plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Local 79 members are already building residential and affordable housing with responsible developers and contractors that pay workers at or above $40 an hour wage and benefit standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: These projects move forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Housing gets built and developers remain successful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: At the same time, workers receive training, health care, retirement security, and wages that allow them to support their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: The problem is not that the industry cannot afford better jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: The problem is that some developers choose a low-road business model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Our community are being harmed by some bad actors in the affordable housing industry who take up government subsidies and pay construction workers poverty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: wages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: They use labor brokers that recruit vulnerable workers, including immigrants, formerly incarcerated people, and economically disadvantaged New Yorkers, pay them near minimum wage without meaningful benefits or job security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: These labor brokers help insulate developers and general contractors from responsibility for the working conditions on their projects when workers report unsafe condition, retaliation, or wage violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Workers are currently organizing and speaking out about a labor broker called Maron Workforce slash Apex Labor Solution, working on subsidized residential projects, including multiple projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Multiple projects developed by Hudson Companies, one of the largest affordable housing developers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Multiple workers have told me they are living in a shelter while working for Marin, so these laborers that build affordable housing can't afford to live in their building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: That's unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: That is unfair to workers and disadvantaged responsible developers and contractors who are already doing the right thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: The city should not allow companies that exploit workers to undercut those that provide safety, family safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: Family sustained careers, especially on projects receiving public subsidies, tax benefits and tax benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: I'll end with this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: The responsible model already exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justice Favor
utterances.text: We need the city to help make it a standard across the residential construction industry.

chapters.summary: Williams shares her personal experience winning a $1.5 million settlement for sexual harassment at a labor broker company, describes being paid $15/hour while pregnant and miscarrying without health insurance, and urges enforcing the Construction Justice Act to protect vulnerable workers from predatory labor brokers.
chapters.title: Tiara Williams (Local 79) on labor broker sexual harassment and exploitation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: We've been here all day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Tiara Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I'm an organizer with Local 79.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Prior to joining the union, I worked for a construction labor broker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I was part of a group of 18 primarily black women workers who won a $1.5 million settlement against our employee for sexual harassment and abuse on the job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: The Attorney General's office found that black women and women of color were systemically targeted by this company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I was subjected to constant harassment from foremen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: The company failed to address repeated complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Instead, they protected sexual abusers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I was making minimum wage and I relied on public assistance benefits, so tax dollars were basically subsidizing this company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I was working for $15 and I was pregnant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: When I miscarried, I had no health insurance and I didn't know if Medicaid was going to cover me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Now as an organizer, I speak to many laborers supplied by brokers on affordable housing projects around the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: These predatorial labor brokers take advantage of workers who are in precarious situations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Formerly incarcerated people, immigrants, and women of color are regularly exploited by these companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: They face the real threat of re-imprisonment if parole officers discover that they are out of work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Complaining about job conditions, sexual harassment, or other mistreatment can cost these workers their freedom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I am fighting to ensure that no one faces the conditions that I experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: I'm fighting to make sure that the bad actors do not find ways to avoid labor standards by using loopholes in the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Residential construction workers should not be excluded from the labor program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: protections that the city has championed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: We must enforce the Construction Justice Act so that the contractors and labor brokers have clear standards for how they treat and pay construction workers who build city subsidized affordable housing developments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tiara Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And you get extra points for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Appreciate your story.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Kevin Kiprovsky, if you're still here, come on up.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Then let's get Anthony Roy side, Eli.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Rayside?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You correct me on the mic.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Anthony Rayside, Eli Perry, Yenen Rodriguez.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Whoever is ready can begin.

chapters.summary: Kaprowski notes older adults are mentioned only twice in the plan, warns that the 1,000-unit senior guarantee is unclear on which program it falls under, that SARA financing has stalled due to Section 8 shortfall, and urges the city not to abandon 100% senior housing in favor of multi-generational models.
chapters.title: Kevin Kaprowski (Live On NY) on senior housing gaps in Block by Block

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify, and thank you for putting me back in the loop when I stepped out for a second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: My name is Kevin Kaprowski, and I'm the Director of Public Policy at Live On New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: We are an organization that represents over 110 community-based nonprofits that provide services under the NYCHA aging portfolio, and we represent most of the senior housing developers in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: In the block-by-block proposal, older adults are mentioned two times, one with a commitment to build 1,000 senior units a year, and two in a multi-generational housing proposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: I want to start with some background.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: We have heard many analyses that older adults are somehow richer than the general population and do not need additional considerations or support, but the reality is the opposite.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: A small group of older Americans may control a huge swath of wealth, but over 50% of older New Yorkers have no retirement savings whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Older adults are most acutely impacted by the housing crisis, affordability crisis, and our broken medical system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Older adults are the fastest growing homeless population, both locally and nationally, and we are concerned that the current housing plan does not recognize the reality of older New Yorkers'lives and is abandoning key programs and supports our older neighbors need to remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: One, the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: 1,000-unit guarantee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: It is not clear under which program that guarantee moves into.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: We have actually heard that because Section 8 is in a drought, they will no longer be financing new SARA programs until they can get guarantees for Section 8.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: We are recommending that the SARA program is guaranteed in some form through the drought, as they've done with other program areas, because older adults are definitely in need of housing that can combine different service areas, and you can only get those efficiencies in 100% senior housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: The second thing is we need increased serving funding and programming for senior housing citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Right now, the only funding is a 30% homeless set-aside service funding for the entire 100% of people in the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: That is not working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: And secondarily, the existing home care crisis means we need to be funding alternative ways to take care of older people in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Next, if we're developing multi-generational housing, we need a focus on older people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Because right now, when we're reading the plan and speaking to people about multi-generational, it seems like the only plan we're hearing is to prevent the development of 100% senior housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: I have a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Which is something we are against because we do believe older adults benefit when all affordable housing is built, but we need specific housing for older adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: And the last thing we need to say is that we believe the administration needs to analyze the data around older adult housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Any analysis that does not recognize the acute crisis of older adult homelessness does not convey an accurate picture of need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: The administration must show that they know the on-the-ground reality and make their decisions with that reality at the fore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Kaprowski
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Rayside shares his personal story of moving from a low-wage labor broker to union construction, describing the economic stability, dignity, and safety he gained. He argues publicly funded projects should not use low-wage labor brokers.
chapters.title: Anthony Rayside (Local 79) on construction career transformation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Swanson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: My name is Anthony Rayside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's all good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I'm from Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I'm a proud Local 79 member and shop steward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I'm here today to voice my support of the Construction Justice Act as part of the mayor's housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: Before I joined Local 79, I worked for one of the labor broker companies that provides labor for residential construction in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I know what it's like to work for a company where you are paid low wage with inadequate benefits for grueling work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I did not have any financial medical stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I could never take my family on vacation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: When I began to work union jobs, the fair wage package, I was actually treated with dignity and told my rights as a worker on a site that took safety seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: Now I don't have to worry about my family in case I get sick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: I'm able to provide my family with economic stability I did not know before, or had before, rather.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: There is no reason that publicly funded projects should use low-wage labor brokers to fulfill their staffing needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: What example is the city setting when they facilitate worker exploitation on construction sites?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: When the city spends our tax dollars to build affordable housing, we need to see those dollars coming back to our communities in the form of local higher jobs with good wages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: The Construction Justice Act is key to ensuring our public funds are spent properly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: Our city needs well-compensated jobs with strong legal protection to give all workers the same voice with stability that the union have given both me and my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Rayside
utterances.text: For your time.

chapters.summary: Rodriguez describes working for labor broker Marin on affordable housing projects developed by Hudson Companies, making $21/hour with inconsistent pay, delayed paychecks, and fear of speaking up about safety or treatment for fear of losing work.
chapters.title: Yael Rodriguez on labor broker experience at Hudson Companies projects

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you for sharing your story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Yael Rodriguez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: I worked for the labor-broken Marin for about a year and a half on affordable housing developed by Hudson Companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: During that time, I find myself trapped in a system that made it extremely difficult to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: The work was inconsistent and I was making around 21 an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: But there were times where my wages would change or my paychecks would just be delayed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: Not knowing if I was going to get paid or what the pay was going to be was very stressful, especially when there were bills and responsibilities that had to be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: But one of the hardest parts was feeling like I couldn't speak up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: I was afraid that if I complained too much about my safety, my pay, or the way I was being treated, I would lose my job or be taken off the schedule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: And that's how work has become trapped, honestly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: You need the paycheck, so you have to keep working, you have to show up, but you're also afraid to speak up because you might lose your work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: But at the same time, if the job doesn't give you stability, protection, or opportunities to build a better future,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: It shouldn't be a reality for any working construction site in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: When we're talking about affordable housing being built with public dollars, as the city prepares to build more housing, we have to make sure that the building is building better opportunities for the workers who are actually building it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: Workers deserve safe jobs, fair wages, stability, and a real pathway to a better future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: We should not have to have a system that keeps workers dependent on labor brokers and afraid to speak up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: We deserve better, and the people building the city future deserve a real opportunity to be a part of that future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yael Rodriguez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Perry shares his story of eight years incarcerated and three years in shelter before finding construction through Pathways to Apprenticeship and Local 79. He urges the city to ensure the housing plan creates middle-class jobs, not poverty-wage labor broker positions, especially for people coming home from incarceration.
chapters.title: Eli Perry on construction career pathway from incarceration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: My name is Eli Perry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: I am a proud union construction worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: I was incarcerated for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: And after coming home, I spent three years living in a shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: I needed someone to give me a real opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: I found that opportunity through Pathways to Apprenticeship,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: and Local 79.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: Construction gave me a job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: It gave me a career, stability, benefits, and a future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: That's why I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: The mayor has an ambition plan to build housing across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: That means thousands of construction jobs and a huge opportunity to move New Yorkers out of poverty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: But right now, too many affordable housing projects rely on labor brokers that hire workers at low wages with little to no benefits and no real pathway to a career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: And the workers they recruit are often people who need opportunity the most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: People coming home from incarceration, immigrants, and New Yorkers struggling to support their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: I could have easily been one of those workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: We cannot spend public dollars to build affordable housing while allowing the workers building it to remain trapped in poverty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: The mayor's housing plan gives us an opportunity to do something different, build affordable housing and build the middle class at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: Give workers the same opportunity that changed my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: Good wages, benefits, training, and a real career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: If we do that, we won't just change the skyline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eli Perry
utterances.text: We'll change people's lives.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, the hearing is over.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No, I'm kidding.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Your stories are really inspiring, and I hope to bring this back to my neighborhood, too, so that we can expand these opportunities and not rely so much on these labor brokers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

chapters.summary: Baker describes witnessing landlords abandoning tenants to mold and cold for profit, and how Our Bronx has successfully intervened in buildings like 2205 Davidson Avenue using community land trust models. He urges passage of both COPA and the Safer Homes Act.
chapters.title: Todd Baker (Our Bronx) on COPA and Safer Homes Act for Bronx buildings

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And whoever is ready.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It's your baby.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: My name is Todd Baker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: I live in Kingsbridge and I work for Our Bronx, where I support our housing justice and community development work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: In that role, I have witnessed the very avoidable harm being done to New Yorkers under our current housing and code enforcement system, most egregiously to communities of color, to seniors whose social infrastructure has been eroded by gentrification and displacement,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: and to those who face language or immigration barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: I work in buildings where landlords have made a calculated decision to abandon their tenants to mold and to cold because it was more profitable for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: Meanwhile, though they are important and they're staffed by hardworking public servants, current enforcement tools like 311 or the alternative enforcement and underlying condition programs fall short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: I know from firsthand experience that there's a better option out there for many of these tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: We have been able to intervene in some of these buildings, like we did with your support, at 2205 Davidson Avenue, or we're doing at 785 East Tremont Avenue, where we are breaking this vicious cycle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: of deteriorating conditions and rising rents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: With the help of experienced development partners, with council members, with HPD, with Neighborhood Restore, with legal services partners, with stakeholders who have a demonstrated commitment to providing high quality affordable housing,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: we have put these buildings on a pathway to a total renovation and to be kept permanently affordable through the Bronx Community Land Trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: This is the sort of transformative change that COPA and Safer Homes could make possible for many more households in dire need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: Both bills have been thoughtfully structured to target the buildings where intervention is most needed and would be most impactful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: Both would leverage the experience of trusted developers, CDCs, and community land trusts to help meet the urgent need to preserve affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: I urge the council to pass both as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Todd Baker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Thomas describes years of no heat, broken elevators, water leaks, stolen packages, roaches and mice at her building, and recounts being told by the owner's son to 'move' if unsatisfied. She urges passage of COPA and the Safer Homes Act.
chapters.title: Stephanie Thomas (3435 Giles Place tenant) on building conditions under Park Cash Realty

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: My name is Stephanie Thomas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: I'm a proud member of R Bronx and a tenant of 3435 Giles Place, Bronx, New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Documentation supports this testimony describing absolute mismanagement by Park Cash Realty of the previous mentioned property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: The following allegations reiterate the maladministration of the aforementioned property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: These examples will emphasize the dire need to pass COPA and the Safer Homes Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: I've resided at this property since October 2015 and strongly believe these initiatives will address the deterioration of our building and community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Some of these are no heat during the winter months, elevator continuously inoperable and unsafe to use when working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Elevator engineer is usually called on average of five times per week.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Water leaks in most apartments, hallways, etc., especially during rainstorms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Faulty patchwork, so problems recur.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Water leaks in the lobby area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Apartments on the seventh floor experience severe water damage due to faulty roof repair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Mailroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: The mailroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Room is unsecured.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Requests for mailboxes for packages are ignored.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Packages are continuously stolen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: Roaches and mice are throughout the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: What's most infuriating is the lack of concern by the owner and his sons in regards to these allegations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: For example, I called about the inoperable elevator in 2016 and was told,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: If I was unsatisfied with the situation, I could move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: This is how Park Cash Realty feels about their tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: The nonchalant attitude about the welfare of tenants depicts the worst kind of apartment ownership in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: COPA and the Safer Homes Act will give legal authority over landlords who neglect their contractual responsibilities and fail to keep their properties safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Thomas
utterances.text: It's time tenants stand up for their rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We need legal support and assistance from our city officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Tenko, a 64-year Bronx resident, describes 16 years of inconsistent heat, broken elevators, and leaks under owner Ved Park Cash, who was named one of the worst landlords. He states that if COPA and Safer Homes had been in place earlier, his building might not have ended up in its current state.
chapters.title: Richard Tenko (3435 Giles Place tenant) on landlord neglect and COPA urgency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: My name is Richard Tenko.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: I will start with the end.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: If COPA had been in place the last time my building was sold, we might never have ended up in the hands of Vant Park Cash.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: If safer homes had been in place, perhaps my building could not have been taken from him a long time ago and we wouldn't be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: I would not be here, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: I urge you to pass both of these bills as soon as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: The name is Richard Tanko.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: I have lived in the Bronx for the last 64 years, the last 26 years at 3435 Giles Place in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: The building has been owned by Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Vet Park Cash, I believe, since 2010.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: That's the reason I am here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Under the ownership of Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Vett Parkash, the expected services of heat during the fall, winter, and spring and a working elevator have been inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: During the heavy rains, it leaks inside the apartments around the windows facing east.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: It also leaks in the lobby and the entrance of the lobby.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Photos and videos of these conditions are available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: When Parkes took ownership of 3435 Giles Place, it was understood that whatever shortcomings had taken place with the building, it would be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Pointing, elevator, heat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: 16 years later, under his ownership, the heat elevator and leaks continued.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: When Parkes took over, we had no idea he had been named one of the top 10 worst landlords in New York City and number one in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Since we had no idea, we gave her the benefit of the doubt and did not form a tenant association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: That was a huge mistake and one we have since corrected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: A tenant in the building was informed that 3435 was in foreclosure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: When ownership and management were asked, they all denied this and refused to prove it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: To provide any information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Our Bronx, a community agency, began to support the 3435 Tenant Association, and I'll leave it as that because, yeah, but you more or less could have an idea what took place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Garcia describes Safer Homes as intervening when landlords fail and buildings fall into severe distress, and COPA as breaking the cycle when buildings change hands. He argues both bills address the housing crisis at two critical points and urges passage.
chapters.title: Edward Garcia (Our Bronx) on COPA and Safer Homes as complementary tools

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Tenko
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you, Rachel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Committee on Housing and Chair Sanchez for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: My name is Edward Garcia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: I'm the co-organizing director of our Bronx, formerly known as Northwest Bronx Community and Clothing Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: And we fight to protect tenants and empower them to fight for safe and dignified housing and long-term community stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: And we work with tenants across the Bronx that are living with mold and vermin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Structural damage as Stephanie and Richard just alluded to and more people will speak to and and they have organized and documented conditions and code 311

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: 1-1 file complaints and attended hearings like this ones before, but too often the cycle continues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Violations accumulate, buildings deteriorate, and tenants are left waiting for meaningful intervention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: And this is why we need Safer Homes Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Safer homes will give the city stronger tools to intervene when buildings are in severe distress and hold negligent landlords accountable like Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Red Park Cash.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: And create pathway towards responsible ownership and long-term stabilization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: And I would add that for our Bronx, responsible ownership also includes tenant ownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Buildings cannot be allowed to remain in limbo while tenants continue living in unsafe conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: We also need to think about what happens when these buildings change hands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: When a neglected, affordable building comes up for sale, COPA creates an opportunity to break that cycle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Rather than simply transferring the building from one owner to another,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: COPA can create an opportunity for responsible, missile-driven organizations, including community land trusts, to purchase and preserve these buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: For tenants, a change in ownership should be an opportunity for something better, to move from neglect to responsible ownership, preserve affordability, and stabilize the building for long term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: At our Bronx, we organize around tenant and community ownership because we know that responsible ownership can preserve affordability, prevent displacement, and strengthen communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Both Safer Homes and COPA give us the tool to address the housing crisis at two critical points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Safer Homes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: help us intervene when landlords fail and buildings fall into severe distress, and COPA gave us an opportunity to potentially break that cycle when those buildings are transferred to responsible ownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Garcia, a 25-year Bronx resident, describes a crumbling roof, leaks in every rain, and slow repairs under new owners. She urges passage of COPA and the Safer Homes Act to remove negligent landlords and improve building conditions. Testimony delivered in Spanish with translation.
chapters.title: Juana Garcia (Spanish testimony) on building conditions and COPA

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Ok, entonces se lo pueden facilitar a ella y ella se lo va traduciendo mientras ustedes hablan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juana García

chapters.summary: Eligio describes mold, collapsed ceilings, cockroaches, and a son with allergies, noting the building was sold overnight without tenant knowledge. She argues COPA would have given tenants and community organizations a chance to participate before the building passed to a new landlord. Testimony delivered in Spanish with translation.
chapters.title: Elizabeth Eligio (Spanish testimony) on building sale without tenant notice
