chapters.summary: Fang, representing 750,000 AARP members in NYC, notes older adults are the fastest growing homeless population, with 60% of older renters rent-burdened. He argues COPA would help older adults age in place by preserving affordable housing and preventing displacement from neighborhoods they've called home for decades.
chapters.title: Lloyd Fang (AARP) on COPA and aging in place

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Thank you so much for this opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: My name is Lloyd Fang, and I am the Associate State Director of Advocacy with AARP New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: I'm here today on behalf of our 750,000 members in New York City and the millions of New Yorkers age 50 and older

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: who call the five boroughs home to indicate that we strongly support the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, and we urge the City Council to pass it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: New York City's housing affordability crisis is clearly an aging issue as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Older adults are the fastest growing age group in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Today, 1.43 million New Yorkers are age 65 or older, a 50% increase since 2000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: At the same time, nearly one in five older New Yorkers lives in poverty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: More than 60% of older adult renter households are rent burdened, meaning they spend more than 30% of their income on housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: For an older New Yorker living on a fixed income, the sale of the apartment building that they live in can bring tremendous uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: A new owner can mean pressure to raise rents, changes in building management and conditions, like some of you have heard already, or displacement from a neighborhood someone has had.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: called home for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: This dynamic is particularly precarious for older New Yorkers and the need to age in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: COPA, of course, can change that dynamic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: By giving qualified nonprofit organizations a first opportunity to purchase certain multifamily buildings, COPA can help move at-risk housing out of the speculative market and preserve it as permanently affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: This is particularly important for our older adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Aging in place is about so much more than just remaining, you know, within the apartment that they know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: It's about staying close to doctors, family members, friends, houses of worship, older adult centers, and the neighbors that they can rely on, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: When an older adult is displaced,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: they lose the communities that they've known and grown accustomed to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Ultimately, what this comes down to is how do we achieve age in place and make it a reality for more and more New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: And with COPO, we can do that, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: We can make New York take a much greater step forward toward fulfilling New York's promise as a city for all ages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Fang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Smith, representing WFSSH which serves 2,500 extremely low-income older adults, warns that the housing plan does not address senior needs at scale. She urges the city to find alternative subsidies for SARA housing during the Section 8 shortfall and not abandon 100% senior housing.

utterances.text: My name is Eustacia Smith.

utterances.text: Wishfish develops and operates housing and provides supportive services to 2,500 extremely low-income older adults, many who are formerly homeless, across a portfolio of 31 buildings in Manhattan and the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eustacia Smith
utterances.text: With 20% of New York City's population being an older adult, well over half with no retirement income, 62% rent burdened, and older adults being the fastest growing homeless population in New York City and the nation, the need to scale up affordable senior housing is clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eustacia Smith
utterances.text: However, we are concerned that the administration's current housing plan does not address the needs of extremely low-income seniors at a time when it is needed most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eustacia Smith
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of our tenants have an AMI of 15% or less.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eustacia Smith
utterances.text: This means traditional tax credit, affordable housing is not an option for them unless they also have a rental subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eustacia Smith
utterances.text: HPD's SARA program, which pairs housing with project-based Section 8, has been a lifesaver for older adults, given that as seniors, their income will only go down as they age.

chapters.summary: Valderrama, a campaign organizer with We Stay/Nos Quedamos in the South Bronx, describes COPA as creating a qualified list of mission-driven nonprofits with a right of first refusal for at-risk buildings, noting over one-third of New Yorkers are rent-burdened and over half in the South Bronx.
chapters.title: Brandon Valderrama (Nos Quedamos) on COPA for South Bronx preservation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: Good evening, good evening, acting chair Wilson, good evening, committee council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: Thank you for extending me the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: My name is Brandon Valderrama.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: I'm a resident and campaign organizer with We Stay Nos Quedamos, a community-based organization in the South Bronx with a penchant for preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: And not just preservation, but now housing affordability as it steps into its role as a CDC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: As a Bronx native, we've experienced many of the things that have been discussed today, whether it be the capital issues around the building more generally, rats, rodents, you name it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: That's been the major topic of discussion today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: And so with that, there's a growing sense of unaffordability and just preservation issues throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: That's the whole reason behind my role, is to bring capital improvements through a coordinated and thorough campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: And that's why I'm here today, urging you to pass Intro 905, the Community to Purchase Act, or COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: COPA creates a qualified list of mission-driven nonprofits, including CLTs, that can step in when certain at-risk...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: multifamily buildings are put up for sales.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: It gives the organization a meaningful opportunity to compete for these properties with a clear timeline and affordability framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: At the heart of COPA is the rights of first refusal, giving qualified nonprofits the skin to stay in the game when it comes to the private market.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: This is especially important because more than one-third of New Yorkers are rent-burdened, and more than half alone are in the South Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: Families are pushed out, and the fabric of the communities change entirely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: COPA is a targeted tool that only targets certain buildings that house tenants that are at risk of displacement and only when an owner chooses to sell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: And I just want to leave off to keep it short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: I urge the city council to pass Intro 905 and give New Yorkers a tool to preserve affordable housing and combat displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Valderrama
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Korczak, SPONY board president, thanks CM Banks for the electronic registration bill and CM Salaam for Intro 717, but opposes COPA, arguing government policies create financial distress that then justifies COPA intervention. chapters.summary: Rivera argues New York cannot build its way out of the affordability crisis, that preserving existing affordable housing is more efficient, and that COPA gives certified nonprofits a real chance to compete for at-risk buildings. He notes the model's success in San Francisco and over five years of Council deliberation.
chapters.title: Juan Rivera (Bilish Preservation, remote) on COPA as proven preservation tool

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Next is Juan Rivero.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Acting Chair Wilson and Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: My name is Juan Rivera, testifying on behalf of Billish Preservation in strong support of COPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: To begin with the obvious, New York is facing an affordability crisis and we cannot build our way out of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: There is little evidence to suggest that building even hundreds of thousands of market rate units would put housing within reach of the low-income households most in need of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: We could build income-targeted affordable housing, and we should, but it is more efficient and easier to preserve existing affordable housing than to build new housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: In a world of limited resources, we need every tool available to tackle a problem of this magnitude.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: For decades, speculative investors have made this problem worse, buying buildings at inflated prices, raising rents, and letting repairs go undone, especially where affordability protections are expiring, and tenants end up paying more for less.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: That's where COPA comes in, by helping restore some degree of balance to a market distorted by speculation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: It gives certified nonprofits a real chance to compete for at-risk buildings when an owner sells, allowing them to preserve much-needed permanently affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: This is not an untested idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: It builds on San Francisco's successful 2019 law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: It is also not a half-baked one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: It reflects over five years of council deliberation and is backed by over 200 affordable housing developers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: land trusts, tenant groups, and lenders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: Every day we wait, more affordable housing is lost to speculation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: I urge you to pass COPA and give New Yorkers a better chance to stay in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Rivera
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: McCleary, a staff attorney at Goddard Riverside's law project, describes working with distressed buildings where landlords are negligent or claim inability to afford repairs. He argues COPA would ensure the next owner is communicative and accountable, and sees it as infrastructure to incentivize more responsible ownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Thank you to the chair, the New York City Council Committee on Housing and Building for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: My name is Justin McCleary, and I'm a staff attorney for the law project at Goddard Riverside, a settlement house serving over 22,000 New Yorkers a year across all ages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Goddard's law project was founded in 1981 to empower tenants and preserve affordable housing through advocacy, legal representation, relationship building, and grassroots education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: I'm grateful to testify regarding Goddard's support for the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: A core part of our tenant organizing work involves identifying distressed buildings where there's already a strong tenant association or where tenants need support building one in order to organize for better building conditions and where needed, develop legal cases against landlords who have failed to make necessary repairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: We often find the buildings our team is working with have landlords who are either negligent or tell tenants that they cannot afford to make these repairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: When an owner will not or cannot maintain safe, healthy housing, they should be encouraged to sell the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: However, the next owner should be one who

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: who will be communicative and accountable to tenants and is committed to working to maintain good living conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: We also see consequences where buildings change hands between owners, such as between LLCs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Rental records can fall through the cracks during these transfers, particularly a transition where a new owner takes over control of a building or when records have not been properly maintained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: In our work with tenants who have recently moved into a building or whose tenancy records have not been maintained properly, we regularly find that their units were originally rent stabilized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Finally, we continue to see private equity and other large-scale investors continuing to grow their ownership of New York City's housing stock.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: These deep-pocketed investors can often move quickly when properties come onto the market, especially through incentives like cash offers to move an offer to closing quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Often, these groups see housing as part of an investment portfolio and are not incentivized to invest in good living conditions and clear communication with tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: The combination of these factors continues to disempower tenants while degrading the quality and quantity of available affordable housing in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: From Goddard's view as a tenant legal service provider and a long-term nonprofit affordable housing developer and provider, we see COPA as a final infrastructure support to incentivize more...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Justin McCleary
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: Oversight hearing on Mayor Mamdani's Block by Block housing plan covering tenant protections, code enforcement, preservation, production, and homeownership, with testimony from HPD Commissioner Levy, DOB Commissioner Tagani, and Director Weaver.

Seven bills considered including COPA (Intro 905), Office of Conversion Assistance (Intro 178), J51 reauthorization (Intro 1015), electronic property registration, building street numbers (Intro 860), owner identification signs (Intro 649), and permit sign-off notices (Intro 717).

Extensive public testimony from over 80 witnesses including tenants, community land trusts, labor unions, property owners, and advocates, with overwhelming support for COPA and strong calls for labor standards on subsidized housing construction.
title: Committee on Housing and Buildings
